title: ESLint Config
body:
Setting up ESLint in a UI project means picking plugins that work with the installed ESLint, turning on the accessibility rules for the framework, and fitting in with TypeScript and Prettier, without replacing what the project already has. Plugins and versions change quickly, so this guide says how to check them, and dates its facts (October 2026).

Start from what the project has

  • An ESLint config is already there (eslint.config.*, or .eslintrc*): extend it, keep its rules, and change only what the task needs.
  • Biome or oxlint already lints the project: adding ESLint duplicates it, so ask first. Both have accessibility rules of their own (Biome's a11y group, oxlint's jsx-a11y rules).
  • No linter yet: propose ESLint with the packages below, and install nothing without the user's OK.

Implement only what the task needs. Add no dependency and run no command, such as an install, the migrator, or --fix, without the user's OK, and use the project's package manager. The project's own rules win; if one conflicts with an accessibility rule here, ask instead of choosing.

Versions

  • ESLint 10 (February 2026) is the only supported line: ESLint 9 reached its end of life on 2026-08-06. ESLint 10 needs Node 20.19, 22.13, or 24 and later.
  • It reads flat config only (eslint.config.*): .eslintrc* and .eslintignore do nothing, and /* eslint-env */ comments are errors. It looks for the config from each linted file's folder up, so a monorepo can have one per package.
  • In a project on ESLint 9 or older, an upgrade is its own task; ask, since its plugins may hold it back (below).

Plugins and the installed ESLint

  • Before adding a plugin, check that its peer range includes the project's ESLint major (npm view <plugin> peerDependencies). npm refuses a plugin whose range doesn't (an ERESOLVE error); --force and --legacy-peer-deps install it anyway, so ask the user instead of using them.
  • As of October 2026, eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y 6.10.2, eslint-plugin-react 7.37.5, and eslint-plugin-import 2.32.0 list ESLint 9 at most, so npm refuses them next to ESLint 10 (checked). Installed with --legacy-peer-deps, their recommended rules ran on ESLint 10.13 on a sample (checked), which isn't support. For React's accessibility rules the user chooses between that, the fork eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y-x (it supports ESLint 10, is at version 0.x, and renames its rules jsx-a11y-x/…), and waiting.
  • These support ESLint 10 and installed cleanly (October 2026): eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7, eslint-plugin-vue 10, eslint-plugin-vuejs-accessibility 2.6, @vue/eslint-config-typescript 14, eslint-plugin-svelte 3, angular-eslint 22, typescript-eslint 8, eslint-config-prettier 10, and eslint-plugin-import-x, the fork for import rules, which are optional.

The config file

  • A new config is eslint.config.mjs, or eslint.config.js when package.json has "type": "module". An ESM eslint.config.js in a package without it still loads on Node 22 and 24, but Node warns (MODULE_TYPELESS_PACKAGE_JSON) and parses it twice (checked). An existing CommonJS config stays CommonJS: require() and module.exports.
  • defineConfig and globalIgnores come from eslint/config. extends takes each plugin's config whole, with its parser and settings, which spreading only its rules into another object leaves out.
  • Ignore the build output (dist/, build/, coverage/); ESLint already ignores node_modules and .git. Browser code gets globals.browser, or no-undef flags window and document.
  • Rules: the recommended configs, plus what the project already enforces. A long list of style rules is a separate decision for the team.

Templates

Each template ran with ESLint 10.13 on a small sample project and reported exactly the problems planted in it (checked).

Browser JavaScript

// eslint.config.mjs: JavaScript that runs in the browser import js from '@eslint/js'; import { defineConfig, globalIgnores } from 'eslint/config'; import globals from 'globals';  export default defineConfig([   globalIgnores(['dist/', 'build/', 'coverage/']),   {     files: ['**/*.{js,mjs,cjs}'],     extends: [js.configs.recommended],     languageOptions: { globals: globals.browser },   }, ]);

React

// eslint.config.mjs: React with TypeScript. Without TypeScript, leave out typescript-eslint. // eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y doesn't list ESLint 10 yet: see "Plugins and the installed ESLint". import js from '@eslint/js'; import { defineConfig, globalIgnores } from 'eslint/config'; import jsxA11y from 'eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y'; import reactHooks from 'eslint-plugin-react-hooks'; import globals from 'globals'; import tseslint from 'typescript-eslint';  export default defineConfig([   globalIgnores(['dist/', 'build/', 'coverage/']),   {     files: ['**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}'],     extends: [       js.configs.recommended,       tseslint.configs.recommended,       reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended,       jsxA11y.flatConfigs.recommended,     ],     languageOptions: { globals: globals.browser },   }, ]);

Without TypeScript, leave out typescript-eslint; jsx-a11y's config turns on JSX parsing. The Rules of Hooks and the React Compiler's checks come from eslint-plugin-react-hooks' configs.flat.recommended; its configs.recommended is still the old format (checked).

Vue

// eslint.config.mjs: Vue 3 with TypeScript, as create-vue sets it up import { globalIgnores } from 'eslint/config'; import { defineConfigWithVueTs, vueTsConfigs } from '@vue/eslint-config-typescript'; import pluginVue from 'eslint-plugin-vue'; import pluginVueA11y from 'eslint-plugin-vuejs-accessibility';  export default defineConfigWithVueTs(   { files: ['**/*.{ts,mts,tsx,vue}'] },   globalIgnores(['dist/', 'coverage/']),   pluginVue.configs['flat/recommended'],   pluginVueA11y.configs['flat/recommended'],   vueTsConfigs.recommended,   {     // By default it wants the control inside the label and linked by id; either one is enough     rules: { 'vuejs-accessibility/label-has-for': ['error', { required: { some: ['nesting', 'id'] } }] },   }, );

As create-vue sets it up. Without TypeScript, use defineConfig from eslint/config with js.configs.recommended, the two plugin configs, and globals.browser. vuejs-accessibility's label-has-for wants a control both inside its label and linked by id unless told otherwise, which flags a correct <label for>; the template accepts either (checked).

Svelte

// eslint.config.mjs: Svelte 5 with TypeScript. Without TypeScript, leave out typescript-eslint // and the last block. import js from '@eslint/js'; import { defineConfig, globalIgnores } from 'eslint/config'; import svelte from 'eslint-plugin-svelte'; import globals from 'globals'; import tseslint from 'typescript-eslint';  export default defineConfig([   globalIgnores(['build/', '.svelte-kit/', 'dist/']),   js.configs.recommended,   tseslint.configs.recommended,   svelte.configs.recommended,   {     languageOptions: { globals: globals.browser },     // The compiler's warnings, its accessibility checks among them; recommended leaves it out     rules: { 'svelte/valid-compile': 'error' },   },   {     files: ['**/*.svelte', '**/*.svelte.ts'],     languageOptions: { parserOptions: { parser: tseslint.parser } },   }, ]);

eslint-plugin-svelte 3's recommended config leaves out svelte/valid-compile, which brings the Svelte compiler's warnings, its accessibility checks among them, into ESLint; the template turns it on (checked).

Angular

// eslint.config.mjs: Angular, as `ng add angular-eslint` writes it, without the selector // prefix rules it adds for the app's prefix import js from '@eslint/js'; import angular from 'angular-eslint'; import { defineConfig } from 'eslint/config'; import tseslint from 'typescript-eslint';  export default defineConfig([   {     files: ['**/*.ts'],     extends: [js.configs.recommended, tseslint.configs.recommended, angular.configs.tsRecommended],     processor: angular.processInlineTemplates,   },   {     files: ['**/*.html'],     extends: [angular.configs.templateRecommended, angular.configs.templateAccessibility],   }, ]);

ng add angular-eslint writes this config, plus selector prefix rules for the app's prefix, and adds the lint builder; ask before running it. Its template accessibility rules are included.

TypeScript

  • typescript-eslint 8 (October 2026) supports TypeScript below 6.1. npm refuses it next to TypeScript 7, which has been latest since July 2026 (checked), and Angular 22 needs TypeScript 6.0. In a project on TypeScript 7, ask the user: stay on TypeScript 6.0 for now, or wait for typescript-eslint's support.
  • Rules that need type information, such as no-floating-promises, come with tseslint.configs.recommendedTypeChecked instead of recommended, and languageOptions.parserOptions: { projectService: true, tsconfigRootDir: import.meta.dirname } (checked). They make linting slower; tseslint.configs.disableTypeChecked turns them off for JavaScript files.
  • TypeScript already checks that imports resolve, so with eslint-plugin-import-x, its named, namespace, default, and no-unresolved rules are off for TypeScript files.

Prettier

Add eslintConfigPrettier, from eslint-config-prettier/flat, as the last entry: it turns off the rules that fight Prettier, such as curly and Vue's max-attributes-per-line (checked). Prettier runs on its own (prettier --check .), not through eslint-plugin-prettier, which Prettier's docs advise against.

Moving from .eslintrc

On ESLint 10, an .eslintrc* config does nothing. ESLint's migrator, npx @eslint/migrate-config .eslintrc.json, writes an eslint.config.mjs and takes in .eslintignore, using FlatCompat from @eslint/eslintrc for configs it can't convert (checked). Ask before running it, install what it lists, then replace each compat.extends(…) with the plugin's flat config where it has one, and check that the old rules still report.

Scripts, editors, and CI

  • Scripts: "lint": "eslint ." and "lint:fix": "eslint . --fix". Flat config finds the file types from files, so --ext is needed only for extensions no files pattern covers.
  • Problems that already exist: list them for the user first. Fixing a whole codebase at once (--fix) is the user's call.
  • VS Code: the ESLint extension finds the flat config, and "editor.codeActionsOnSave": { "source.fixAll.eslint": "explicit" } fixes on save. It lints JavaScript, TypeScript, and Vue files without more settings; Svelte files need "svelte" in eslint.validate, which then lists every language to lint.
  • CI: if the project has CI, run the lint script there with the project's Node version. Don't add a CI service it doesn't have.

Troubleshooting

  • A parsing error in .vue or .svelte files with TypeScript: the TypeScript parser isn't set for them (the templates set it).
  • A rule that throws "context.getSourceCode is not a function" or similar: the plugin uses APIs ESLint 10 removed. Check its peer range; fixupPluginRules() from @eslint/compat can bridge it, after asking.
  • Slow linting: rules with type information. Turn them off for JavaScript files, and lint only changed files before a commit.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] The project's lint setup was checked first: an existing ESLint config is extended and keeps its rules, and with Biome or oxlint in place the user was asked before ESLint was added
  • [ ] Every package added was agreed with the user and added with the project's package manager
  • [ ] Each plugin's peer range includes the installed ESLint major, or the user chose what to do about it
  • [ ] The config is flat config, in eslint.config.mjs unless package.json has "type": "module" (then eslint.config.js)
  • [ ] An .eslintrc config was moved with the migrator, keeps its rules, and uses the plugins' flat configs where they have them
  • [ ] Browser globals are set, and build output is ignored
  • [ ] The framework's accessibility rules are on: jsx-a11y for React, vuejs-accessibility for Vue, the Svelte compiler's warnings through svelte/valid-compile, and Angular's template accessibility config
  • [ ] With TypeScript, typescript-eslint's configs are used, and rules that need type information have projectService
  • [ ] With Prettier, eslint-config-prettier is the last config, and Prettier runs on its own
  • [ ] The lint script runs on every file type the project has, without crashes or parsing errors
  • [ ] Problems that already exist were listed for the user, and nothing was fixed in bulk without the user's OK
  • [ ] The lint script runs in the project's existing CI, if it has one
  • [ ] Editor settings, if any, use "source.fixAll.eslint": "explicit"
excerpt: ESLint for UI projects: build on the lint setup the project has, flat config for ESLint 10, the framework's accessibility rules, TypeScript and Prettier, and plugins checked against the installed ESLint.

title: Form Validation Pattern - UX and Timing Strategies
body:
Validation decides how a form feels. Errors that appear too early nag, errors that appear too late waste time, and errors only some people can perceive lock the others out. This pattern says when errors appear, what they say, and where focus goes, with the project's form library or without one. It targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a form library, such as React Hook Form, TanStack Form, Formik, VeeValidate, Angular forms, or SvelteKit Superforms, or a schema library, such as Zod, Valibot, or Yup, apply this timing and these messages through it, and keep its rules.
  2. Without one, use the browser's constraint validation: required, type, pattern, min, max, and minlength in the markup, read through field.validity, with the app's own messages.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Setting up a form library for this timing (check the project's version):

  • React Hook Form 7: the defaults (mode: "onSubmit", reValidateMode: "onChange") show errors after a submit attempt and clear them as people fix them. To also show format errors before that, call trigger(name) on blur when getFieldState(name).isDirty is true and the field isn't empty, and on change while getFieldState(name).invalid is true: before the first submit, the defaults don't check a field again as it changes. Until formState.isSubmitted, clear a field's error with clearErrors(name) when it's emptied, since "required" waits for a submit attempt. mode: "onTouched" comes close, but also flags required fields someone only tabbed through.
  • VeeValidate 4: set when fields are checked with validateOnBlur, validateOnChange, validateOnInput, and validateOnModelUpdate, globally with configure() or per field, and show a required error only once the form's submitCount is above 0. Version 3's mode: "lazy" is gone.
  • Angular forms: show a control's error when the form was submitted, or when the control is dirty and touched and its error isn't required. The value updates on each input, so the error goes as soon as it's fixed.
  • Schema libraries, such as Zod, Valibot, or Yup: keep the rules in the schema, and map its messages to the field errors and the summary.

When errors appear

  • Nothing shows while the form loads, or while someone tabs through it to read it.
  • A field someone typed in is checked for format errors when they leave it.
  • "Required" errors wait for a submit attempt, even for a field someone typed in and emptied. After that attempt, every error shows, required ones included.
  • Once a field shows an error, it's checked on every input, so the error goes the moment the value is right. Emptied before a submit attempt, it shows no error.
  • Dependent fields follow the same rule: no "Passwords must match" while the confirmation is still being typed.
  • Async checks, such as an available username, run once typing pauses (about 500 ms, suggested), with "Checking…" in the status region. Only the latest request's answer counts: number each request, or abort the previous one with an AbortController.
  • CSS :user-invalid comes close: in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit it matched after typing an invalid value and leaving, and after a submit attempt, also with novalidate, and not after tabbing past an empty field. But it also matches a required field someone typed in and emptied, as they leave it (checked). So style aria-invalid, which follows the app's timing; use :user-invalid only when the browser's validity is the only source.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

// When errors appear. A field the person typed in is checked when they leave it, and a field // that shows an error is checked again on every input, so the error goes as soon as it's // fixed. "Required" errors wait for a submit attempt, so tabbing through a form, or emptying // a field, shows none. showError(field, message) stands for the field's error display, and // message(field) for the app's wording of field.validity. const form = document.getElementById('signup'); let edited = new WeakSet(); form.noValidate = true; // the app's messages replace the browser's; without script, the browser checks  // Shows the field's error, or clears one it shows; fields without errors are left alone function check(field) {   if (!field.willValidate) return;   const waiting = field.validity.valueMissing && form.dataset.submitted !== 'true';   const text = field.validity.valid || waiting ? '' : message(field);   if (text || field.getAttribute('aria-invalid') === 'true') showError(field, text); }  // Runs fn after a reset that wasn't cancelled. The form puts its values back only after its // reset event, and a listener after this one can still cancel the reset. function afterReset(fn) {   form.addEventListener('reset', (event) => setTimeout(() => {     if (!event.defaultPrevented) fn();   })); }  form.addEventListener('input', (event) => {   edited.add(event.target);   if (event.target.getAttribute('aria-invalid') === 'true') check(event.target); }); form.addEventListener('focusout', (event) => {   if (edited.has(event.target)) check(event.target); }); // A reset starts over: no errors, and no field counts as typed in afterReset(() => {   edited = new WeakSet();   form.querySelectorAll('[aria-invalid="true"]').forEach((field) => showError(field, '')); });

What errors say

  • What's wrong and how to fix it, with the field's label: "Enter your full name", "Enter an email address in the correct format, like name@example.com". Not "Invalid input", and not a library's technical message.
  • In text next to the field, in its aria-describedby, with aria-invalid="true" on the field. Color and an icon only add to the text.
  • Keep what the person typed; never clear a field because it's wrong.
  • Errors from the server show the same way, at the field they belong to, or in the summary for the form as a whole.
  • Never reveal private facts. "Email already registered" tells anyone who has an account. Availability checks are for public names, such as usernames or handles, and the server rate-limits them.

Required and optional fields

Say it in words. When most fields are required, mark the optional ones "(optional)", and say so at the top of the form. If the design uses an asterisk, explain it at the top, and don't color it like an error. Required fields have the required attribute, which screen readers announce.

Submitting

  • The submit button stays enabled before a submit attempt and after a failed one, so people can find out what's missing.
  • A submit attempt checks every field. With errors, the form isn't sent:
    • Short forms (a few fields, all visible): focus moves to the first invalid field.
    • Longer forms: an error summary at the top, "There is a problem", lists each error as a link to its field, and focus moves to the summary's heading. Following a link moves focus to the field (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit).
  • Focus is the announcement: no live region repeats the errors. An error that appears when someone leaves a field may be announced once through the form's one polite status region; field errors are never role="alert".
  • Focusing a field scrolls it into view. With a sticky header, scroll-padding-top on the scrolling element keeps the field clear of it (WCAG 2.4.11).
  • While the form is sent, the button gets aria-disabled="true" and ignores another press, and the status region says "Sending…". The disabled attribute would drop focus from the button, or from a field where someone pressed Enter. On success, go on; on failure, keep everything typed, show the error, and make the button work again.
  • The snippet above sets novalidate from script, so the app's messages replace the browser's only when the app runs. Without script, the browser still checks the form.
<!-- The first thing in a longer form, hidden until a submit attempt finds errors --> <div class="error-summary" hidden>   <h2 tabindex="-1">There is a problem</h2>   <ul></ul> </div> 
// On submit: check every field. With errors, the form isn't sent, and focus moves to the // error summary's heading when the form has one (longer forms), or else to the first invalid // field. Each summary link goes to its field (#id), and following it moves focus there. // Register the app's own submit handler after this one: it runs only for a valid form. form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {   form.dataset.submitted = 'true'; // from now on, "required" errors show too   const fields = [...form.elements].filter((field) => field.willValidate);   fields.forEach(check);   const invalid = fields.filter((field) => !field.validity.valid);   const summary = form.querySelector('.error-summary');   if (summary) summary.hidden = invalid.length === 0;   if (invalid.length === 0) return;   event.preventDefault();   event.stopImmediatePropagation();   if (!summary) return invalid[0].focus();   summary.querySelector('ul').replaceChildren(...invalid.map((field) => {     const link = Object.assign(document.createElement('a'), { href: `#${field.id}`, textContent: message(field) });     const item = document.createElement('li');     item.append(link);     return item;   }));   summary.querySelector('h2').focus(); }); // A reset starts over: the summary goes, and "required" waits for the next submit attempt afterReset(() => {   delete form.dataset.submitted;   const summary = form.querySelector('.error-summary');   if (summary) {     summary.hidden = true;     summary.querySelector('ul').replaceChildren();   } });

Resets

  • Most forms don't need a reset button: it's easy to press by mistake, and it loses everything typed. Apps often reset a form from script after sending it, though, so these rules hold either way.
  • After a reset that wasn't cancelled, everything worked out from the values is rebuilt from the restored values, as on page load: the errors and the summary go, no field counts as typed in, "required" waits for the next submit attempt, and sections follow their answers.
  • The form puts its values back only after its reset event, without input or change events, and a listener after yours can still cancel the reset. So wait for the event to finish, and check defaultPrevented first: afterReset() in the first snippet does both.

Fields that don't always apply

  • Put a section that only some answers need in a <fieldset>, and while it doesn't apply, make it hidden and disabled. Disabled fields are left out of validation and of the form data (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit), so they can't block the submit.
  • Clear the section's errors when it hides.
  • The section follows its answer on page load, on change, and after a reset. A reset puts the answer back without a change event, and leaves the section's own hidden and disabled as they were.
  • Don't skip fields only because they're visually hidden: custom controls often hide their native input and still need its validation.
<!-- A section only some answers need: hidden and disabled while it doesn't apply --> <input type="checkbox" id="for-company" name="for-company"> <label for="for-company">I'm buying for a company</label> <fieldset id="company-details" hidden disabled>   <legend>Company details</legend>   <label for="company">Company name</label>   <input id="company" name="company" required aria-describedby="company-error">   <p class="field-error" id="company-error" hidden></p> </fieldset> 
// A section that doesn't apply is hidden and disabled: disabled fields are left out of // validation and of the form data, so they can't block the submit. Its errors go when it // hides. It follows its answer on load, on change, and after a reset, which puts the answer // back without a change event. showError() and afterReset() as above. const answer = document.getElementById('for-company'); const section = document.getElementById('company-details');  function sync() {   section.hidden = !answer.checked;   section.disabled = !answer.checked;   if (section.disabled) {     section.querySelectorAll('[aria-invalid="true"]').forEach((field) => showError(field, ''));   } }  answer.addEventListener('change', sync); afterReset(sync); sync(); // the answer the page starts with, such as a saved one, counts too

Multi-step forms

  • Check each step when someone tries to move on, as a submit, with only that step's fields (its fieldset's elements), and stay on the step while it has errors. Earlier steps stay enabled, so they're sent with the form; a step that an answer skips is disabled, like a section that doesn't apply.
  • On a new step, move focus to its heading (tabindex="-1"), so its title and instructions are read, and update the page title, such as "Delivery address, step 2 of 4".
  • Don't ask again for something given in an earlier step: fill it in, or offer it to choose (WCAG 2.2 3.3.7).
  • Before a legal, financial, or data-changing submission, let people review and correct everything (WCAG 3.3.4).

Formats

  • Accept common formats and normalize them, such as spaces in card numbers and dashes in phone numbers.
  • Show the expected format in hint text, not in a placeholder, which disappears on typing.
  • Dates follow the person's locale. For a date people know by heart, such as a birthday, three fields (day, month, and year) work better than a picker.

Edge cases

  • The click after an error: when an error appears as someone leaves a field to press the submit button, the button moves under the pointer before the mouse is released, and the click is lost (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). The form is invalid anyway, and the error shows. To keep the click, keep room for one error line under the fields above the button.
  • Sections that don't apply are hidden and disabled, so they aren't checked or sent (see "Fields that don't always apply").
  • Autofill and paste count as typing.
  • Server-rendered forms that reload with errors put the summary at the top, move focus to it on load, and start the page title with "Error:".
  • Several forms on a page: each has its own summary and status region.

Examples

  • Email: someone types "john@" and moves on; the error "Enter an email address in the correct format, like name@example.com" appears. As they type "example.com", it goes the moment the address is complete.
  • Required field: someone tabs past an empty Full name field to read the form, and nothing appears. They type a letter, delete it, and move on: still nothing. They submit, and "Enter your full name" appears, with focus on the field.
  • A section that doesn't always apply: "I'm buying for a company" shows the Company details section and enables it; unticked, the section hides, is disabled, and loses its errors, and the form can be sent without it.
  • Password confirmation: nothing shows while the confirmation is typed. If it doesn't match when they leave it, "Passwords must match" appears, and goes as soon as it matches.
  • Username availability: after a 500 ms pause in typing, "Checking…" in the status region, then "Username available" or "That username is taken. Try another" next to the field. An older answer that arrives late is ignored.
  • Checkout, a longer form: a submit with three errors shows the summary "There is a problem" at the top, with links to the three fields, and focus on its heading.
  • Multi-step form: Next checks the step; with errors it stays, and without, focus moves to the next step's heading "Delivery address", with the name from step 1 already filled in.
  • Card number: the hint says "The 16 digits on the front of your card"; spaces typed between groups are accepted and removed.
  • Date of birth: three fields, day, month, and year, in the person's locale order, rather than a date picker.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Tabbing through the form without typing shows no errors
  • [ ] A field someone typed in shows a format error when they leave it, and the error goes as soon as the value is right
  • [ ] "Required" errors appear only after a submit attempt, even for a field someone typed in and emptied, and then for every empty required field
  • [ ] A section that doesn't apply is hidden and disabled, so it never blocks the submit; its errors go when it hides, and it follows its answer on load and after a reset
  • [ ] A form reset clears the errors and the summary, forgets which fields were typed in, and holds "required" back again; a cancelled reset changes nothing
  • [ ] A failed submit moves focus to the error summary's heading on a longer form, or to the first invalid field on a short one, and each summary link moves focus to its field
  • [ ] Errors are text next to their fields, connected with aria-describedby and aria-invalid, and say how to fix the problem
  • [ ] No field error is a live region, and screen readers hear each error once
  • [ ] The submit button stays enabled until sending starts, then uses aria-disabled, keeps focus, and ignores another press
  • [ ] With script, the browser's own error messages don't appear; without it, the browser still checks the form
  • [ ] Required and optional fields say so in words
  • [ ] Async checks wait for a pause, say "Checking…", and only the latest answer counts
  • [ ] Multi-step forms move focus to each step's heading and never ask twice for the same information
  • [ ] A focused field is never hidden under a sticky header
  • [ ] A form library, if the project has one, is set up to give the same timing

See also

  • Text Input Field: the label, hint, and error wiring of each field.
  • Select and Combobox: required choices, and typed text that isn't a choice.
  • Login & Registration Forms: these rules in sign-in and registration forms.
  • Modal Dialog: forms in a dialog.

These are suggestions; the pattern works with any form components.

title: Dark/Light Mode
body:
Dark mode is easy to start and easy to get subtly wrong: a flash of the other theme on every load, a choice that's forgotten, a control nobody can read, form fields that stay white, and borders that vanish in one theme. This pattern covers the preference and where it's applied, the color tokens, the control, and media, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project already has themes (a theme provider, a design system's dark mode, Tailwind's dark variant), extend them to meet this guide instead of adding a second system. Keep their API and storage key.
  2. Otherwise add a short script in the head, color tokens, and a theme control.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

The preference

  • Three choices: Light, Dark, and System, which follows the system's setting (prefers-color-scheme). System is the default.
  • The choice is saved under the app's own storage prefix (acme.theme), or in a cookie when the server renders the page. A value the app doesn't know counts as System.

Before the first paint

  • A short blocking script, first in <head> before the stylesheets, reads the saved choice and sets data-theme="light" or "dark" on <html>. Applied later, in a framework's mount or effect, the other theme paints first.
  • Reading storage can throw where it's blocked (a SecurityError in a sandboxed frame, in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, checked), so it's wrapped in try/catch, and the page then follows the system's setting.
  • The script also sets <meta name="theme-color">, which colors the browser's toolbar on phones. Under a Content-Security-Policy it needs the page's nonce or its hash.
  • Server-rendered apps put the script where the framework writes the head (Next.js: the root layout; Nuxt: app.head; SvelteKit: app.html). The attribute it sets differs from the server's HTML, so React needs suppressHydrationWarning on <html>; or the server reads a cookie and renders the right theme.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<!-- First in <head>, before the stylesheets: the saved choice is applied before the first paint.      "acme" stands for the app's own storage prefix. Under a Content-Security-Policy, the script      needs the page's nonce or its hash. --> <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> <meta name="theme-color" content="#ffffff"> <script>   (() => {     let choice = 'system';     try {       choice = localStorage.getItem('acme.theme') ?? 'system';     } catch {       // Storage can be blocked; the page then follows the system's setting     }     // Light or Dark as chosen; anything else follows the system's setting     const dark = choice === 'dark' || (choice !== 'light' && matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches);     document.documentElement.dataset.theme = dark ? 'dark' : 'light';     document.querySelector('meta[name="theme-color"]').content = dark ? '#121212' : '#ffffff';   })(); </script> 
/* color-scheme: light dark follows the system's setting, without script too, and the script's    data-theme pins one. Each token has its light and its dark value. */ :root {   color-scheme: light dark;   --color-background: light-dark(#ffffff, #121212);   --color-surface: light-dark(#f5f5f5, #1e1e1e);   --color-text: light-dark(#111111, #eeeeee);   --color-text-muted: light-dark(#666666, #999999);   --color-border: light-dark(#e0e0e0, #333333); /* dividers only */   --color-border-strong: light-dark(#767676, #8a8a8a); /* fields and controls: 3:1 */   --color-accent: light-dark(#0066cc, #4da6ff); } :root[data-theme="light"] {   color-scheme: light; } :root[data-theme="dark"] {   color-scheme: dark; } body {   background: var(--color-background);   color: var(--color-text); }

Colors

  • Colors are tokens by purpose (background, surface, text, muted text, border, strong border, accent), each with a light and a dark value, and components use the tokens, never raw colors.
  • color-scheme: light dark on :root with light-dark() follows the system's setting even without script, and data-theme pins color-scheme to one theme, which also switches form controls and scrollbars (checked: an input's background in all three engines). light-dark() has been in every current browser since 2024; for older ones, repeat the tokens under [data-theme="dark"].
  • Contrast holds in both themes: 4.5:1 for text, and 3:1 for the borders of fields and controls (1.4.11). Thin dividers can be lighter (#e0e0e0 is 1.3:1 on white), so controls get a stronger border token (#767676, 4.5:1). Check the project's own colors in both themes.
  • Dark backgrounds are usually a dark gray, such as #121212, rather than black, and saturated colors are toned down; both are suggestions, and the project's palette wins.
  • Tailwind follows the attribute with @custom-variant dark (&:where([data-theme=dark], [data-theme=dark] *)); in its CSS (version 4), or darkMode: ['selector', '[data-theme="dark"]'] in its config (version 3.4.1 and later).

The theme control

  • Three choices are a radio group (a <fieldset> with the legend "Theme") drawn as a segmented control, or a menu of three radio items. Two themes are one button with aria-pressed and a label that stays the same ("Dark theme"). A button that cycles through three states doesn't say what the next press does.
  • Icons beside the words are decorative; with icons only, each option still has its name.
  • A choice applies at once and holds for the page, which keeps it in memory; it's saved where storage works, so a save that fails, with storage blocked or full, loses nothing on the page. Under System, the theme follows the system's setting as it changes: a matchMedia listener fires in all three engines (checked).
  • The control shows the saved choice at load, again on pageshow (after Back, Chromium restores the checked radio after the page's scripts have run, checked), and when another tab saves a choice or clears storage (the storage event, whose key is null after a clear).
  • A page restored from the back/forward cache takes the saved choice only if what storage holds changed while it was away (a removed choice is a change, not saved System), so a choice that couldn't be saved isn't lost (checked in Chromium's back/forward cache).
  • Without script, the control stays hidden, since it couldn't do anything. Choosing announces nothing more: the radio says its new state.
<!-- The theme choice, shown by the script: a radio group drawn as a segmented control --> <fieldset class="theme-choice" hidden>   <legend>Theme</legend>   <div class="theme-options">     <label><input type="radio" name="theme" value="light"> Light</label>     <label><input type="radio" name="theme" value="dark"> Dark</label>     <label><input type="radio" name="theme" value="system" checked> System</label>   </div> </fieldset> 
/* A radio group drawn as a segmented control: the radios stay real, so the arrows move between    them, and each label shows the state */ .theme-choice {   border: 0;   margin: 0;   padding: 0; } .theme-options {   border: 1px solid var(--color-border-strong);   border-radius: 999px;   display: inline-flex;   padding: 4px; } .theme-options label {   border-radius: 999px;   cursor: pointer;   padding: 6px 12px;   position: relative; } .theme-options input {   inset: 0;   margin: 0;   opacity: 0;   position: absolute; } .theme-options label:has(input:checked) {   background: var(--color-text);   color: var(--color-background); } /* :focus, not :focus-visible: WebKit doesn't match :focus-visible on a radio the arrows moved to */ .theme-options label:has(input:focus) {   outline: 2px solid var(--color-accent);   outline-offset: 2px; } /* Forced colors replace backgrounds, so the chosen option takes the system's highlight */ @media (forced-colors: active) {   .theme-options label:has(input:checked) {     background: Highlight;     color: HighlightText;     forced-color-adjust: none;   } } 
// The theme choice: Light, Dark, or System. A choice applies at once and holds for this page, and // is saved where storage works; System follows the system's setting as it changes; and the // control matches the saved choice after Back and when another tab changes or clears it. The // colors repeat the head script's. const KEY = 'acme.theme'; const control = document.querySelector('.theme-choice'); const inputs = [...control.querySelectorAll('input')]; const systemDark = matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)'); let choice = 'system'; // nothing saved (null) or a value the app doesn't know counts as System let stored = null; // what storage held when this page last read or wrote it, null for nothing  // What storage holds, or this page's own choice where storage can't be read function saved() {   try {     return localStorage.getItem(KEY);   } catch {     return choice;   } }  function apply() {   const input = inputs.find((option) => option.value === choice) ?? inputs.find((option) => option.value === 'system');   input.checked = true;   const dark = input.value === 'dark' || (input.value === 'system' && systemDark.matches);   document.documentElement.dataset.theme = dark ? 'dark' : 'light';   document.querySelector('meta[name="theme-color"]').content = dark ? '#121212' : '#ffffff'; }  control.addEventListener('change', (event) => {   choice = event.target.value;   try {     localStorage.setItem(KEY, choice);     stored = choice;   } catch {     // Not saved where storage is blocked or full; the choice still holds on this page   }   apply(); }); systemDark.addEventListener('change', apply); // Another tab saved a choice, or cleared storage (an event without a key) addEventListener('storage', (event) => {   if (event.storageArea !== localStorage || (event.key !== KEY && event.key !== null)) return;   choice = stored = saved();   apply(); }); // After Back, Chromium restores the checked radio after this script has run, so the choice is // applied again. A page restored from the back/forward cache takes the saved choice only if // storage changed while it was away, so a choice that couldn't be saved isn't lost. addEventListener('pageshow', (event) => {   const now = event.persisted ? saved() : stored;   if (now !== stored) choice = stored = now;   apply(); }); choice = stored = saved(); control.hidden = false; apply();

Media

  • Logos and icons need to show in both themes: an inline SVG with currentColor, a second asset, or <picture> with prefers-color-scheme sources, which follow the system's setting rather than the saved choice. filter: invert(1) suits single-color dark logos only; it turns an orange logo blue.
  • Images with white backgrounds can sit on a surface, or be dimmed slightly in the dark theme.
  • A favicon for dark tabs: <link rel="icon" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">.

Motion

Colors change at once. Elements with hover transitions also animate when the theme changes; if that looks wrong, turn transitions off for a frame while switching, with a class on <html>. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, a theme change never animates, View Transitions included.

Forced colors

In forced colors, the system's colors replace the tokens. Nothing depends on a color or a background image alone, and the chosen option in the control takes Highlight.

Edge cases

  • Several tabs: a choice in one applies in the others.
  • Frames from other sites keep their own theme; pass it as a parameter where they take one.
  • Charts and code highlighting need their own colors in each theme.
  • An app that has only a dark theme sets color-scheme: dark and offers no control.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] The saved choice is applied in the head, before the first paint, so no load or reload shows the other theme first
  • [ ] Light and Dark apply as chosen; System, nothing saved, or a value the app doesn't know follows the system's setting
  • [ ] Where storage is blocked or full, nothing breaks: the page follows the system's setting or the saved choice, and a new choice holds until the page closes, also when the page comes back from the back/forward cache
  • [ ] Under System, the theme follows the system's setting when it changes, without a reload
  • [ ] The control offers Light, Dark, and System as a radio group or a menu of the three, or for two themes one button with aria-pressed; no button cycles through three states
  • [ ] The control shows the saved choice at load, after Back, and when another tab changes or clears it
  • [ ] color-scheme matches the theme, so form controls and scrollbars follow it, and so does theme-color
  • [ ] Without script, the page follows the system's setting and the control is hidden
  • [ ] Colors are tokens with a light and a dark value, and components use the tokens
  • [ ] Text meets 4.5:1 and the borders of fields and controls 3:1 in both themes; thin dividers may be lighter
  • [ ] Focus indicators show in both themes
  • [ ] Logos, icons, and images stay visible in both themes
  • [ ] In forced colors, the page uses the system's colors and the chosen option stays visible
  • [ ] Under reduced motion, a theme change doesn't animate
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Button: buttons and their focus rings in both themes.
  • Navigation Bar (Responsive) with Mobile Menu: the header that usually holds the theme control.
  • Modal Dialog: dialogs and their backdrop in both themes.
  • Form Validation Pattern - UX and Timing Strategies: error and success colors that meet contrast in both themes.

These are suggestions; the pattern works on its own.
excerpt: Light, dark, and System themes that never flash: the saved choice applied before the first paint, tokens that set color-scheme, a radio group to choose, and System following the system's setting as it changes.

title: AI Response Rendering Pattern
body:
An assistant's reply arrives as a stream of events: text, tool calls and their results, citations, artifacts, and with some providers a reasoning channel. This guide turns that stream into a stable, readable message that's safe to show, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA. It covers the inside of one assistant message. The chat around it, with the transcript, the composer, and its Send and Stop button, is the AI Agent Chat Layout's job, and approving actions with consequences is the AI Action Review Pattern's. This guide works with or without them.

Start from what the project has

  1. Find the project's message renderer, its Markdown renderer, and its sanitizer, and build on them. Keep their APIs.
  2. If the project's AI SDK already sends typed message parts, such as text, tool calls, and sources, map them to the blocks below instead of parsing text.
  3. Choose the block types and controls the task needs. Leave out the rest.

Add no dependency, such as a Markdown parser, a sanitizer, or a syntax highlighter, without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility, security, or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Blocks

A reply is an ordered list of blocks, each with a stable id, a type, a state, its content, and details. Key blocks by id, never by index. An unknown type renders as a labelled block of plain text, never dropped.

  • text: prose, through the Markdown renderer. It may hold citation markers, and its links are underlined.
  • code: a fenced code block with its language. It renders before its closing fence arrives, has a Copy code button, and gets syntax highlighting once it's final.
  • tool-call: a tool the assistant calls, with its result.
  • citation: a source the text refers to.
  • artifact-ref: something shown elsewhere, such as a document, a file, or a chart.
  • error: a failure, shown in place.
  • reasoning (optional): only when the provider exposes a reasoning channel and the product chooses to show it.

The reply's states

  • idle: no reply yet.
  • queued: the request is accepted, and the first content hasn't arrived. The host shows its waiting indicator.
  • streaming: blocks are added, or the trailing block grows.
  • tool-running: a tool call is running.
  • awaiting-review: a tool call with consequences is held until someone approves it. The reply waits for the person, not for the model.
  • complete: finished; every block is final.
  • cancelled: stopped by the person; what arrived stays.
  • errored: failed; what arrived stays, with an error block.

A reply moves from idle to queued when the message is sent, and to streaming on the first content. It moves between streaming and tool-running as tools run, to awaiting-review when a tool call is held, and back when the call is approved (tool-running) or rejected (streaming, with the card cancelled). From any of these it ends as complete, cancelled on Stop, or errored on a failure it can't recover from.

Streaming

  • Text deltas grow the trailing text block, and code deltas the trailing code block; another type starts a new block. Tool-call updates change their card by id, never by recreating it.
  • Collect deltas, update the DOM at most once per animation frame, and flush before the reply ends.
  • Re-render only the trailing block, from its full text, with a Markdown renderer that tolerates unclosed fences, partial links, and partial emphasis. Finished blocks never re-render. For long replies, re-parse only the last paragraph of the trailing block.
  • A CSS-only caret sits at the end of the growing block while the reply is streaming or running a tool. It hides while the reply awaits review and once it ends. It's steady, or blinks for 5 seconds at most (WCAG 2.2.2).
  • Don't animate tokens; whole blocks may fade in.

The snippets in this guide are plain JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

// Deltas can arrive many times per frame. Collect them and update the DOM at most once per // animation frame. trailingText stands for the growing block's element; with Markdown, // re-render only that block from its full text instead of appending. let pending = ''; let frame = 0;  function onTextDelta(delta) {   pending += delta;   if (!frame) frame = requestAnimationFrame(flush); }  // Also call flush() before the message becomes complete, cancelled, or errored function flush() {   cancelAnimationFrame(frame);   frame = 0;   if (pending) trailingText.append(pending); // append() adds text, never HTML   pending = ''; }

Keeping model output safe

Model output is untrusted: prompt injection can put anything in it.

  • Render Markdown through a sanitizer: no raw HTML from the model, or only an allowlist of harmless elements and attributes.
  • Links work only for absolute http, https, and mailto URLs. Anything else, including relative links, renders as text. Links to other sites get rel="noopener noreferrer", and a link that opens a new tab says so.
  • Images load only from hosts the product allows. Any other image URL could carry conversation data in its query string to another site, without anyone clicking, so render it as a link with its alt text. The same goes for link previews the product fetches on its own. A Content-Security-Policy img-src is a second line of defense.
  • Tool inputs and results, file names, and citation titles render as text.
  • An artifact rendered as HTML or SVG goes in an iframe with the sandbox attribute, without allow-same-origin, and with allow-scripts only if it has to run code; ideally from a separate origin. The sandbox doesn't stop it from loading images, styles, or fonts from any host, which would send data out the same way. So give its document a Content-Security-Policy that allows requests only to hosts the product allows, such as default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; img-src https://images.example.com: as a header when it's served from its own origin, or as the first element of a srcdoc document. A srcdoc iframe also inherits the page's own policy. An artifact that runs code also needs script-src for that code, such as 'unsafe-inline' in a srcdoc document.
  • An artifact can also navigate its own frame to any URL, with data in the URL: through a link the person clicks, or, with allow-scripts, by its code or a meta refresh. Its own policy can't stop that, so the page that embeds artifacts limits frame-src to the origins it embeds on purpose, such as frame-src https://artifacts.example.com, or to 'none' when every artifact is a srcdoc document; a srcdoc artifact still loads and runs under it.
// Model output is untrusted. Links work only for absolute https, http, and mailto URLs, and // images load only from hosts the product allows. Anything else renders as text, and an // image from another host as a link with its alt text. imageHosts stands for that list. const imageHosts = new Set(['images.example.com']);  function safeLinkUrl(href) {   try {     const url = new URL(href); // no base URL, so a relative link throws and renders as text     return ['https:', 'http:', 'mailto:'].includes(url.protocol) ? url.href : null;   } catch {     return null;   } }  function safeImageUrl(src) {   const href = safeLinkUrl(src);   return href?.startsWith('https:') && imageHosts.has(new URL(href).hostname) ? href : null; }

Tool calls

Each tool call is a card that changes in place by its id. It shows a readable tool name (not the internal id), a status line in text, and disclosures for the input (labelled fields or JSON) and the result.

  • pending: the name and a muted placeholder.
  • running: status text with a subtle indicator, static under reduced motion.
  • success: a one-line summary, such as a count or a title, with the full result behind the disclosure.
  • error: what failed, with details behind the disclosure, and Retry when it's safe. The rest of the reply continues.
  • cancelled: a cancelled label.

Citations

  • The marker is a link to the source (<a href>), since it navigates. Its name starts with its visible number, such as "1: Example Article, example.com" (WCAG 2.5.3).
  • A preview with the title, the domain, and a short snippet shows on hover and focus. It meets WCAG 1.4.13: Escape closes it, the pointer can move onto it, and it stays until the pointer or focus leaves. The popover attribute keeps it in the top layer, so overflow can't clip it.
  • A reply with three or more sources ends with a list of them.
  • A marker without a source is left out, never shown as a bare number.

Artifacts

Something too big for the message, such as a document, a file, or a chart, shows as a card with its title, its type, and an Open button. Opening it shows the artifact in a side panel, a drawer, or full screen, moves focus there, and returns focus to the card on close. The card works as soon as it appears.

Reasoning (optional)

  • Show reasoning only when the provider exposes a reasoning channel and the product chooses to show it. Otherwise there's no reasoning block, not even an empty one.
  • By default it's a short status, such as "Thought for 4s".
  • Show the full text only when the provider's terms allow it and the product needs it: as a disclosure, collapsed by default. The answer stays visually first.

Errors

Errors show in place, under what arrived, which stays.

  • Connection lost: Retry from where it stopped if the API supports it, otherwise Regenerate.
  • Rate limit: Retry, with an optional countdown that's announced once, not every second.
  • Refusal: show the refusal as the reply's content; never cut it silently.
  • Tool failure: in the tool-call card's error state; the reply continues.
  • Timeout: Retry.
  • Cut off at the length limit: Continue, if the API supports it.

Controls

  • At the foot of a finished reply: Copy (the Markdown source), Regenerate, and Good and Bad response buttons (aria-pressed) with an optional comment. Retry sits on an error block.
  • They show on focus as well as on hover, and always on touch screens. Icon buttons have names, such as "Copy response", and are at least 24 by 24 px. On phones, more than three go in a More actions menu.
  • Stop: in a chat, Stop is the host's: its send button turns into Stop and calls this pattern's stop, which keeps what arrived. Without a host Stop, show Stop at the foot of the streaming reply, available at once, and turn it into Regenerate in place when the reply ends.
  • Edit belongs to the person's message, which the host renders.
  • Share is product-dependent. Before creating a link, say what it includes and who can open it.

Announcements

One element with role="status" per conversation, present before anything changes, announces one short sentence at a time. In a chat the host renders it and this pattern announces through it; used on its own, this pattern renders it. While a modal dialog is open over the conversation, the region is inert, and anything to announce goes through a region inside the dialog.

  • "Acme Assistant is responding" when the reply starts
  • the tool step while one runs, such as "Searching the web"
  • "Response complete", "Response stopped", or the failure at the end

The streamed text is never announced; a setting can optionally read each finished reply aloud. Streaming and lifecycle changes never move focus. A visually hidden heading at the start of the message (the host's, in a chat) lets people find the reply after "Response complete".

Scrolling

The host's scroll area follows new content only while the reader is at the bottom. Once they scroll up, it stays put and offers a jump to the latest content. In the AI Agent Chat Layout the layout does this; elsewhere, the host does.

Small screens and motion

  • On narrow screens, cards stack their parts, citation previews stay inside the viewport, and code blocks scroll sideways instead of wrapping.
  • Motion is optional: whole blocks fade in over 200 ms, tool-call cards change background or border over 150 ms, and citation previews fade in over 120 ms. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, nothing blinks or fades, the running indicator is static, and scrolling never animates.

Performance

  • Coalesce deltas within one animation frame.
  • Re-render only the trailing block, and keep finished blocks from re-rendering (memoize them by id).
  • Highlight code once its block is final, and load citation previews on hover or focus.
  • Virtualize long conversations at the host, not inside one message.

Working with the other AI guides

  • With the AI Agent Chat Layout: the layout owns the shell, the transcript and following new content, the waiting indicator, the Send and Stop button, Edit on the person's messages, the person's messages, and the conversation's status region. This pattern owns the blocks inside each assistant message, the cursor, the cards, Copy, Regenerate, feedback, and Retry, and what to announce through the layout's status region. The layout's waiting indicator hides as soon as this pattern's cursor appears.
  • With the AI Action Review Pattern, for tool calls with consequences, such as sending messages, changing records, payments, or sharing files:
    • The tool call stays pending until reviewed, and the reply moves to awaiting-review. The card's status line says it's waiting for approval, and the cursor and the running animation stop.
    • Approval moves the action to approved. The card turns running only when the action starts running, cancelled on rejection, and error when running it fails, while the rest of the reply continues.
    • Undo, retry, partial failures, and the audit trail belong to the review pattern; the card only reflects the result.
    • The review's announcements go through the same status region, never a second announcer, except while the review is a modal dialog: the page behind it is inert, so the review announces through its own region inside the dialog.
    • Only tool calls the product classifies as without consequences skip review: already authorized, read-only, sending no sensitive data out of the product, and costing nothing meaningful.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] A streaming reply shows a cursor at its end that goes away when the reply completes, stops, or fails, and never blinks for longer than 5 seconds
  • [ ] Markdown with an unclosed code fence renders as a code block while it streams
  • [ ] Many deltas within one frame cause one DOM update, and finished blocks don't re-render
  • [ ] A tool call's card moves through pending, running, and success or error in place, with its state in text
  • [ ] A tool call held for approval puts the reply in awaiting-review: no cursor, no running animation, and Stop still works
  • [ ] Stop keeps what arrived, and a dropped connection shows an error under the partial content with Retry
  • [ ] Rate limits, refusals, timeouts, and truncation each show their own message
  • [ ] In model output, scripts never run, javascript: and relative links render as text, and nothing loads from, or navigates to, a host the product doesn't allow, including from inside an HTML artifact
  • [ ] A citation marker is a link whose name starts with its number; its preview opens on hover and focus and closes with Escape, and three or more sources get a list
  • [ ] A screen reader hears when a reply starts, runs a tool, ends, or fails, and never hears the streamed text
  • [ ] Copy, Regenerate, feedback, and every disclosure have names, work from the keyboard, and are at least 24 by 24 px
  • [ ] No reasoning surface shows when the provider doesn't expose reasoning; when one shows, it's a short status, collapsed by default
  • [ ] With reduced motion, nothing blinks, fades, or scrolls smoothly
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens, and text and controls meet the contrast minimums in light and dark themes

See also

  • AI Agent Chat Layout: the chat shell this pattern fits into.
  • AI Action Review Pattern: the approval surface for tool calls with consequences.
  • Toast Notifications: feedback outside the message, such as a failed Copy.
  • Modal Dialog: confirmations, and the full-screen view of an artifact.
  • Dark/Light Mode: theme tokens that keep cards, previews, and code readable in both themes.

These are suggestions; the pattern works with any chat shell.
excerpt: How to render an AI assistant's reply as it streams: Markdown, code, tool-call cards, citations, artifacts, and optional reasoning, with a Stop that keeps partial text, errors shown in place, and model output treated as untrusted. Companion to the AI Agent Chat Layout.

title: AI Action Review Pattern
body:
When an AI assistant wants to do something with consequences, such as sending an email, changing records, or paying an invoice, people need to see what it will do and decide before it happens. This guide defines that review: what to show, how approval scales with risk, and what happens during and after the run. It targets WCAG 2.2 AA. It works on its own, and with the AI Agent Chat Layout and the AI Response Rendering Pattern, which define the conversation and the assistant's messages.

Start from what the project has

  1. Build on the project's dialog, drawer, button, checkbox, disclosure, and table components, and its permission and audit services. Keep their APIs.
  2. Choose what the task needs: the review surfaces, partial approval, editing, pause, undo, and the audit trail. Leave out the rest.

Add no dependency, such as a focus-trap library or a form library, without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility, security, or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

The guide covers reviewing one action, a batch, or a plan before it runs; risk labels; approve, reject, edit, pause, stop, retry, and undo; task-scoped permission requests; progress; and the audit trail. It doesn't cover back-end authorization, policy engines, model safety, legal approval workflows, or background agents that run without anyone watching.

The action model

Turn the agent's proposal into typed action items, never generated prose alone. Each has a stable id (never key rows by index), a title, a plain-language summary of its consequence, an action type, a risk level, its reversibility, the objects it affects, the permissions it needs, its inputs and destination, what led to it, its state, an idempotency key once it's approved, and audit details.

Action types: message (send, post, publish, notify), record-update, file-operation, schedule, code-change, payment-or-order, external-api, and system-setting. An unknown type still renders as a reviewable item, clearly labelled, and is never approved automatically.

Risk levels

Risk shows as text and an icon, never color alone. It sets how much review an action gets.

  • low: reversible, local, expected, limited in scope
  • medium: changes shared data, several targets, or saved state
  • high: external, sensitive, costly, changes permissions, destructive, or hard to undo
  • blocked: invalid, missing a permission, failing a policy check, unsupported, or missing a prerequisite

Reversibility is reversible, partially reversible, irreversible, or unknown. Treat unknown as higher risk.

The review

  • Header: the goal in plain language ("Update 12 overdue invoices"), the status, the highest risk among the selected actions, and the main controls.
  • Plan summary, before any details: what will happen, why the agent suggests it, what data or tool results it's based on, whether it can be undone, and how many steps or how long. When the proposal follows content from outside the product, such as an email, a web page, or a shared file, say so and link to it: instructions inside such content may not come from the user.
  • Action list: each action's title and summary, what it affects (records, files, recipients, settings), where it goes, the permission it uses, its risk and reversibility, a preview or diff where there is one, and a checkbox when partial approval is supported.
  • Details, behind disclosures: input parameters, the tool and integration, the raw payload, policy checks, the evidence behind the proposal, and audit details.

The review can be a card in an assistant's message (for low-risk actions), a side panel (for plans of several actions), a drawer or sheet (on phones and tablets), a dialog (for urgent, high-risk, or irreversible confirmations), or full screen (for long plans and dense diffs).

Controls

  • Approve runs the selected eligible actions. Name it for the action and its scope, such as "Send to 3 recipients" or "Update 43 records", as a dialog names its primary action.
  • Approve selected runs only the checked actions, and never the others.
  • Reject declines the plan. Edit opens the parameters, the message text, the selected objects, or the constraints, validated with the project's form rules. Ask for revision sends a correction back to the assistant.
  • Pause and Stop are reachable as soon as actions run. Stop starts no new action; one already sent may still finish, and its result shows.
  • Retry runs failed or skipped actions again, Undo reverts completed ones when there's a rollback path, and View log opens the audit trail.

Confirmation rules

  • Low risk: one Approve button, when the affected objects and reversibility are visible.
  • Medium risk: show the affected objects and reversibility before approval, and allow editing where parameters matter.
  • High risk: an explicit step that states the consequences, never just "Are you sure?", with focus on the least destructive action.
  • Irreversible: a typed confirmation that accepts paste, or a separate step that names the consequence. Don't use hold-to-confirm: holding is hard for many people with motor impairments, and has no standard keyboard or screen reader behavior.
  • Blocked: approval isn't available, and the review says what must change before it can be.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<label for="confirm-phrase">To confirm, type <strong>delete 43 records</strong></label> <input id="confirm-phrase" autocomplete="off" spellcheck="false"> <button type="button" id="confirm-action" aria-disabled="true">Delete 43 records</button> 
// Paste works: the point is a deliberate step, not a typing test. The button stays // focusable (aria-disabled, not disabled) and ignores activation until the phrase // matches. approve() stands for the app's approval request. const input = document.getElementById('confirm-phrase'); const button = document.getElementById('confirm-action'); const phrase = 'delete 43 records';  input.addEventListener('input', () => {   const matches = input.value.trim().toLowerCase() === phrase;   button.setAttribute('aria-disabled', String(!matches)); });  button.addEventListener('click', () => {   if (button.getAttribute('aria-disabled') !== 'true') approve(); });

The run's lifecycle

The review moves through these states: proposed, reviewing, needs-changes (after an edit or a request for revision, until the agent sends a revised plan), approved (and not yet started), executing, paused, completed, partially-completed, failed, cancelled, and reverted. Each action has its own state: proposed, selected, blocked, approved, executing, completed, failed, skipped, cancelled, or reverted.

  • Only eligible proposed actions can be selected; blocked ones stay visible but can't be.
  • An action that depends on another shows that, and is skipped if the other fails.
  • Selections survive opening and closing details.
  • A state change never replaces the reviewed plan or its partial results.

Failures, retries, and undo

  • After a failure, every action stays visible with its own state, and completed, failed, skipped, cancelled, and reverted actions look different.
  • Retry runs only failed or skipped actions, and only when it's safe. It never reruns a completed action unless the person chooses to.
  • Each approved action gets an idempotency key, and every retry sends the same key, so the server runs the action at most once.
  • Give each request a time limit. Only an answer from the app decides the outcome: no answer, after a timeout or a dropped connection, or an error from a gateway (502 to 504) instead of the app, leaves it unknown, since the action may have run. Say that instead of "Failed", and retry only with the same key, or after checking the status.
  • An answer that only accepts the action, such as 202 Accepted or a pending status in the app's answer, isn't the end. The action stays executing, with its Pause and Stop, and the review tracks it until the app reports how it ended.
  • Before Undo, show what it will revert. If the rollback fails, keep that state and show how to escalate.
// One idempotency key per approved action, reused on every retry, so the server can tell a // retry from a new request and never runs the action twice. runAction() stands for the app's // request: it sends the key, for example in an Idempotency-Key header, and resolves with the // server's response. async function execute(action) {   action.idempotencyKey ??= crypto.randomUUID();   let response;   try {     response = await runAction(action, { idempotencyKey: action.idempotencyKey, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) });   } catch {     // No answer, after a timeout or a dropped connection: the action may still have run     action.state = 'failed';     action.failure = 'outcome-unknown';     return;   }   // 202 Accepted: the app has the action but hasn't finished it, so track it until it reports   if (response.status === 202) action.state = 'executing';   else if (response.ok) action.state = 'completed';   else {     action.state = 'failed';     // A gateway's error (502 to 504) doesn't say whether the app ran the action     action.failure = response.status >= 502 && response.status <= 504 ? 'outcome-unknown' : 'error';   } }

Permissions and the audit trail

  • Show the permission scope in plain language, and why this action needs it. Prefer one-time or task-scoped access to broad, lasting grants, and offer a manual path when permission is denied and the workflow allows it.
  • The server checks the permission and the approval again: hiding or disabling a control is a convenience, not security.
  • Record audit events for proposals, approvals, rejections, edits, runs, failures, cancellations, retries, and rollbacks. Each records the action and review ids, the actor and the approver, the time, the tool or integration, the permission scope, an input summary or hash, an output reference, the state changes, the failure reason, and the rollback result.
  • Show a short activity log by default, with technical details behind disclosures.

Accessibility

  • Use headings for the review title, the plan summary, the action list, and the audit trail. Each selectable action's name contains its title and consequence, and aria-describedby connects it to its consequence, permission, and reversibility.
  • A modal review follows the Dialog guide: native <dialog> opened with showModal(), or the rest of the page inert. Focus goes to the heading or the first safe control, and returns to the invoking control on close. Escape closes it as Cancel and never approves; in a high-risk confirmation step, Escape cancels the step and returns to the review.
  • An inline, side-panel, or drawer review moves focus to its heading when it opens. Progress updates never move focus.
  • A validation failure moves focus to the first invalid field, and a permission failure to the explanation or the scoped request. After Undo, focus stays near the affected action.
  • Lifecycle updates, such as executing, completed, failed, cancelled, and reverted, are announced through one polite status region: the conversation's, when the review sits in a chat, otherwise its own. A modal review makes everything outside it inert, which hides the conversation's region, so while it's open it announces through a status region inside the dialog. Use role="alert" only for urgent failures, and never stream progress logs into a live region.
  • Space toggles selections and disclosures, Enter activates buttons, and nothing runs when an action is selected or a parameter edited.
  • Controls are at least 24 by 24 px, or have enough space around them.

Layouts

  • From 1024 px: a side panel, a split view, or full screen for dense plans; the summary and the action list can sit beside the details.
  • 768 to 1023 px: the summary above the action list, with dense details behind disclosures.
  • Below 768 px: a full-height sheet or full screen, with sticky main controls and safe-area padding. Set scroll-padding-bottom to the controls' height, so they never cover the focused field, an error, or a status message.
  • Long action lists can be filtered by risk, state, or selection.

Motion

Motion is optional. State changes use a short background or border transition (150 ms), and surfaces follow the project's drawer, sheet, or dialog motion. Progress shows state without constant motion. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, progress and state changes don't animate, and the status text stays.

Working with the other AI guides

  • The AI Agent Chat Layout owns the shell, where review cards sit in the conversation, and the conversation's status region. Low-risk reviews render as cards in the transcript; high-risk or dense plans move to a side panel, drawer, or dialog.
  • The AI Response Rendering Pattern owns tool-call cards and their states (pending, running, success, error, cancelled). A tool call with consequences stays pending while this pattern reviews it, and the reply waits in its awaiting-review state. Approval moves the action to approved, and the card turns running only when the action starts running, cancelled on rejection, and error when running it fails.
  • This pattern owns the review, the action model, the risk and confirmation rules, the run, partial failures, the audit trail, and permission requests.
  • Only tool calls the product classifies as without consequences skip review: already authorized, read-only, sending no sensitive data out of the product, and costing nothing meaningful. Reads that send sensitive query data to external services, call metered APIs, or need new permissions are reviewed like any other action.

Examples

  • Sending an email: the recipients, subject, body, attachments, the context it came from, and when it sends, with external recipients flagged. People can edit the text, remove recipients, save it as a draft, approve, or ask for a softer tone.
  • A bulk record update: 43 proposed customer updates grouped by risk, with a sample diff and selectable rows. People approve the low-risk changes and reject one high-risk change.
  • Scheduling: attendees, time zone, conflicts, conferencing, external guests, the agenda, and whether personal calendar access is used. People can change the time or the attendees before approving.
  • Sharing a file: the file, its current access, the proposed recipients, the access level, any expiry, inherited permissions, and whether the share can be revoked. A public link needs explicit confirmation.
  • A code change: the touched files, the diff, the commands the agent wants to run, the permission to run them, the test plan, and how to roll back. Commands run only after approval.
  • A payment or an order: the amount, account, recipient, invoice, due date, fees, and whether it can be cancelled, with high-risk confirmation and audit logging.
  • A permission request: the exact missing scope, why this action needs it, for how long, and a manual alternative when there is one.
  • A partial failure: five actions were approved. Three completed, one failed validation, and one was skipped because it depended on the failed one. The review stays visible, with Retry for the failure and Undo for the completed actions.
  • No answer: the request to send an invoice times out, or its connection drops. The action says it's unknown whether the invoice was sent, and Retry reuses its idempotency key, so the server sends it at most once.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Proposed actions show before anything runs, each with what it affects, where it goes, the permission it uses, its risk in text and an icon, and whether it can be undone
  • [ ] Low, medium, high, and blocked actions get the review the confirmation rules give them, and blocked actions can't be approved
  • [ ] Approve is named for the action and its scope, and Approve selected runs only the selected actions
  • [ ] An irreversible action's typed confirmation accepts a pasted phrase, and its button stays focusable and does nothing until the phrase matches
  • [ ] Reject, Edit, and Ask for revision work, and edited values are validated with the project's form rules
  • [ ] Pause and Stop are reachable as soon as actions run, and Stop starts nothing new
  • [ ] After a partial failure, every action shows its own state (completed, failed, skipped, cancelled, or reverted), and Retry runs only failed or skipped actions
  • [ ] An action whose request gets no answer, after a timeout or a dropped connection, says its outcome is unknown, and retrying it reuses its idempotency key, so it never runs twice
  • [ ] An action the app accepts but hasn't finished (202 Accepted) stays executing, with Pause and Stop, until the app reports how it ended
  • [ ] Undo says what it will revert, and its result is recorded
  • [ ] The audit trail records the action, actor, approver, time, tool, permission scope, inputs, outputs, outcome, and rollback
  • [ ] A modal review works like the Dialog guide: focus moves in, the page behind is inert, Escape cancels without approving, and focus returns to the control that opened it
  • [ ] An inline or side-panel review moves focus to its heading when it opens, and progress updates never move focus
  • [ ] Screen readers hear lifecycle changes once each, without the progress log
  • [ ] Sticky controls on phones never cover the focused field, an error, or a status message
  • [ ] With reduced motion, progress and state changes don't animate, and the status text stays
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens, and risk labels, text, and controls meet the contrast minimums

See also

  • AI Agent Chat Layout: places review cards in the conversation.
  • AI Response Rendering Pattern: renders the tool-call cards that hand off to the review.
  • Modal Dialog: for urgent or blocking confirmations.
  • Toast Notifications: completion, retry, and undo feedback after the review has closed.
  • Command Palette: commands with consequences can go through the same review.
  • Data Table: bulk actions and selectable affected objects.
  • Form Validation Pattern: editable action parameters.
