  • Dark/Light Mode: risk labels and status colors that stay readable in both themes.
  • Button: approve, reject, destructive, busy, and icon-only buttons.

These are suggestions; the pattern works in any agent workflow.
excerpt: A framework-agnostic pattern for reviewing AI-proposed actions before they run: plan preview, risk labels, scoped permissions, approve, reject, and edit controls, undo, progress, and an audit trail.

title: Landing Page Layout (Marketing)
body:
A landing page explains an offer and leads to one action. Its common mistakes are about trust and access: invented testimonials, calls to action whose names don't match their text, a sticky header over the focused link, and entrance animations that leave sections blank. This guide covers the page from the header to the footer, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a header, sections, cards, or buttons, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend them to meet this guide. Keep their APIs.
  2. Otherwise build it from plain HTML: a <header>, a <main> with a <section> for each part, and a <footer>.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Content

  • The page uses the user's real copy, testimonials, client logos, and numbers. Where the task doesn't give them, use placeholders that look like placeholders, such as "[Customer quote]" and "[Name, role, company]", and ask for the real ones.
  • Never invent testimonials, customer names, logos, ratings, or statistics. Invented social proof misleads visitors, and fake reviews and testimonials are against consumer protection rules in the US and the EU.

Structure

  • The page is a <header>, a <main>, and a <footer>. In <main>, each part is a <section> named by its heading (aria-labelledby): the hero, the features, social proof, an optional pricing section, and a closing call to action.
  • The hero's headline is the page's only <h1>; each section has an <h2>, and cards inside a section have <h3> titles.
  • The page itself scrolls; no section scrolls on its own.

The header

  • The header starts with a skip link, "Skip to content", shown while it has focus and going to <main id="main" tabindex="-1"> (WCAG 2.4.1). Then the logo, a link to the home page named with the site's name, a <nav> labelled "Main", and one call to action.
  • position: sticky; top: 0 keeps the header at the top without a script and keeps its space in the page. A fixed header takes no space, so the page would need padding that matches its height. scroll-padding-top on the root element, set to the header's height, scrolls focused elements and in-page link targets clear of it (WCAG 2.2 2.4.11).
  • Optional: the header starts transparent over the hero and turns solid once the page has scrolled past a threshold. The hero is pulled up under the header by the header's height. An IntersectionObserver on a sentinel at the top of the page, as tall as the threshold, switches it, with no scroll listener. At exactly the threshold, the sentinel's edge still touches the window, so the header turns solid one pixel later (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). Without script, the header stays solid.
  • The header's text meets 4.5:1 in both states: in the transparent state against the hero behind it, the lightest part of a hero image included.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version. The header's links, dropdowns, and menu are in the Navigation Bar guide.

<!-- The sentinel is as tall as the distance the page scrolls before the bar turns solid --> <div class="scroll-sentinel" aria-hidden="true"></div> <header class="site-header">   <a class="skip-link" href="#main">Skip to content</a>   <a class="logo" href="/">Acme</a>   <!-- the site's <nav> (the Navigation Bar guide) and the call to action --> </header> <main id="main" tabindex="-1">   <section class="hero" aria-labelledby="hero-title">     <h1 id="hero-title">Reports your whole team reads</h1>     <!-- the subtitle, the calls to action, the product image -->   </section>   <!-- the other sections --> </main> 
/* The bar sticks with CSS alone and keeps its space. The hero is pulled up under it, so the bar    can start transparent over the hero, and the page scrolls focused elements and link targets    clear of it. */ :root {   --site-header-height: 64px; } html {   scroll-padding-top: var(--site-header-height); } .site-header {   background: var(--surface);   min-height: var(--site-header-height);   position: sticky;   top: 0;   transition: background-color 300ms;   z-index: 10; /* the sticky-bar layer of the project's scale */ } .site-header.is-transparent {   background: transparent; /* its text meets 4.5:1 against the hero behind it */ } .hero {   margin-top: calc(-1 * var(--site-header-height));   padding-top: calc(var(--site-header-height) + 48px); } .scroll-sentinel {   height: 48px; /* the bar turns solid after 48 px of scrolling */   pointer-events: none;   position: absolute;   top: 0;   width: 1px; } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {   .site-header {     transition: none;   } } 
// The bar is transparent while the sentinel at the top of the page is in view, and solid once // the page has scrolled past it. An IntersectionObserver switches it, so nothing runs while the // page scrolls; without script, the bar stays solid. const header = document.querySelector('.site-header'); new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {   header.classList.toggle('is-transparent', entry.isIntersecting); }).observe(document.querySelector('.scroll-sentinel'));

The menu on small screens

  • Below 1024 px, the links move into a menu opened by a Menu button, and from 1024 px the header shows them: one switch, as in the Navigation Bar guide.
  • The menu is a native <dialog> opened with showModal() and named "Main menu", so the rest of the page is inert, Escape closes it, and focus returns to Menu. It has a visible Close button ("Close menu"), and closes when a link in it is followed.
  • A click on the backdrop closes it as in the Modal Dialog guide: the <dialog> has no padding of its own (an inner wrapper has it), so only the backdrop makes the dialog the click's target, and the press has to start on the backdrop too. A rule that checks only the target also closes the menu on a click on its padding, and on a drag from inside it onto the backdrop (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit).
  • Menu and Close are at least 44 px square on touch screens.

Calls to action

  • A call to action that goes to a page (sign up, book a demo, see pricing) is a link (<a href>). A button is only for an action on this page, such as opening a dialog.
  • Its visible text says where it goes ("Start free trial", "Book a demo"), and nothing replaces that text as its name: an aria-label that differs from the visible text fails WCAG 2.5.3, since voice control users say what they see. Where two calls to action read the same but go to different places, add visually hidden words after the visible text ("Get started", then hidden "with Professional").
  • One primary call to action per section; the secondary one is outlined or a text link.

The hero

  • The headline, a short subheadline, the calls to action, and a product image or video. On phones they stack in that order; from 1024 px, text and media sit side by side.
  • The headline and the image are visible at load. They're usually the Largest Contentful Paint, so they don't fade in from opacity 0.
  • The hero image is never lazy-loaded and gets fetchpriority="high". Every image gets width and height, so nothing shifts while images load, and srcset with sizes when it comes in several widths.
  • Text over an image gets an overlay or a scrim that keeps it at 4.5:1, checked over the lightest part of the image.
  • A background video is muted and playsinline, has a visible pause button (WCAG 2.2.2), and doesn't play on its own under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, where its poster image shows. A demo video with speech has captions.

Features

  • A grid from CSS alone, such as repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(16rem, 100%), 1fr)), or one, two, and three columns at 768 and 1024 px. It needs no resize handler.
  • Each card has a decorative icon (aria-hidden="true"), an <h3>, and a short description.
  • More than six features: a second row, not a carousel or tabs. A carousel hides features behind controls, and one that turns on its own needs a pause button (WCAG 2.2.2).

Social proof

  • A testimonial is a <figure> with the quote in a <blockquote> and the name, role, and company in a <figcaption>. The name isn't a heading. An avatar beside the name is decorative (alt=""), or the name is read twice.
  • Client logos are a list of images, each named after its company ("Acme"), not "logo".
  • Numbers (customers, uptime, ratings) come from the user, with their source; they're claims like any other.
  • With no testimonials yet, leave the section out, or show a logo list; never fill it with invented quotes.

Email signup

  • Optional, in the hero or the closing section. The field has a visible label, not just a placeholder, type="email", and autocomplete="email"; the text says what people sign up for and how often they'll hear from you.
  • Its result ("Check your inbox to confirm") and its errors go to one polite status region that's in the page from the start; a field error goes in the field's description, as the Form Validation Pattern says.

Motion

  • All motion is optional. The scroll reveal fades sections in as they reach the window. It hides only what it can show again: sections still below the window once the page has loaded and the browser has restored its scroll position, on screens, when motion is allowed. After a reload or Back, WebKit restores the position only after the load event, so a section hidden earlier blinks out and fades back in (checked). Without script, under reduced motion, and when printing, nothing is hidden.
  • It observes with threshold 0 and no root margin. A threshold is a share of the section, so with 0.1 a section taller than ten windows never shows, and a root shrunk at the bottom never meets a short last section at the end of the page (both checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). Focus in a section shows it at once: a waiting section skips the fade, which would start it at opacity 0, and a fade that's under way ends, through transition: none on the section while it has focus. That rule covers every section, not only fading ones, so a transition the project gives the section doesn't fade it in either, and it has to win over that transition. It has to be none: only a property that leaves transition-property cancels its running transition, and a zero duration leaves the fade running (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit).
  • The hero never fades in, since it holds the largest paint.
  • Smooth scrolling for in-page links goes in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference). Turn each animation off where it's defined, rather than with one rule for every element: a reset that removes all animations leaves keyframe-based reveals stuck on their first frame.
  • A hover lift on cards and buttons is optional; under reduced motion, use a color change instead.
/* Sections fade in as they scroll into view: only on screens, and only when motion is allowed.    The script marks the sections it hides (.is-waiting); without it, nothing is hidden. */ @media screen and (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {   .reveal.is-waiting {     opacity: 0;     translate: 0 16px;   }   .reveal.is-fading-in {     transition: opacity 600ms ease-out, translate 600ms ease-out;   }   /* Focus in a section shows it at once, over this fade or any transition the project gives the      section. "none", not a shorter duration: only a property that leaves transition-property      cancels its running transition. It comes last, to win over .is-fading-in. */   .reveal:focus-within {     transition: none;   } } 
// Hides only what it can show again: sections still below the window once the page has loaded // and the browser has restored its scroll position (WebKit does that after the load event), so // nothing in view ever disappears. Threshold 0 and no root margin, so a section taller than the // window, and a short one at the very end of the page, still show. Focus shows a waiting // section at once; the CSS ends a fade that's under way. function setUp() {   const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {     for (const entry of entries) {       if (!entry.isIntersecting) continue;       entry.target.classList.replace('is-waiting', 'is-fading-in');       observer.unobserve(entry.target);     }   });   for (const section of document.querySelectorAll('.reveal')) {     if (section.getBoundingClientRect().top < innerHeight) continue; // in view, or above it     section.classList.add('is-waiting');     observer.observe(section);   } } document.addEventListener('focusin', (event) => event.target.closest('.reveal')?.classList.remove('is-waiting')); if ('IntersectionObserver' in window) {   const later = () => requestAnimationFrame(() => requestAnimationFrame(setUp));   if (document.readyState === 'complete') later();   else addEventListener('load', later, { once: true }); }

Layers

Layers, bottom to top: the page, sticky bars, dropdowns and popovers, toasts, then modals, which make the rest of the page inert. The project's layering scale wins; native <dialog> and the popover attribute use the top layer and need no z-index. The header is a sticky bar, and the menu is a modal.

Small screens and overflow

  • At 320 px wide nothing scrolls sideways, and long headlines wrap (overflow-wrap: break-word).
  • Don't hide overflow on sections. overflow-x: hidden makes the other axis compute to auto, so the section becomes a scroll container, and a sticky element inside it sticks to the section instead of the page (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). Fix what overflows; if something has to be cut, overflow-x: clip doesn't make a scroll container.
  • On phones with a notch, env(safe-area-inset-top) pads the header only when the viewport meta tag has viewport-fit=cover; without it, the values are 0.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • Content up to 1200 px wide, centered; section padding 96 px from 1024 px and 48 px on phones; grid gaps 32 px and 24 px.
  • The headline 48 to 64 px from 1024 px and 32 to 40 px on phones, line height 1.1 to 1.2; section headings 32 to 40 px; body text 16 to 18 px at line height 1.5.
  • Calls to action at least 24 px tall, 44 px suggested, with a 2 px focus outline at a 2 px offset.
  • Colors: headings #111827 (17.7:1 on white), body text #374151 (10.3:1), muted text #4b5563 (7.6:1, and 7.2:1 on a #f9fafb section). A primary call to action with white text needs #2563eb (5.2:1); #3b82f6 is only 3.7:1, and a green one needs #047857 (5.5:1), since #10b981 is 2.5:1. The footer's text on #f9fafb is #4b5563; #6b7280 on #f5f5f5 is only 4.4:1.

Edge cases

  • No testimonials yet: leave the section out, or show a list of client logos; never invent them.
  • Many features: a second row of cards, not a carousel.
  • A long headline: it wraps on phones; shorten it before making the text smaller than 32 px.
  • Before the script runs: every section is visible and the header is solid. Below 1024 px the menu needs the script, so keep the main pages reachable without it too, such as from the footer.
  • A pricing section: the Pricing Table guide covers the billing choice and the plans.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] The page starts with a skip link to the main area, and has one h1, the hero's headline, with an h2 for each section
  • [ ] The header sticks with CSS alone, and a link focused under it, or a section reached by an in-page link, is scrolled clear of it (scroll-padding-top at its height)
  • [ ] A header that starts transparent over the hero turns solid once the page has scrolled past the threshold, stays solid without script, and its text meets 4.5:1 in both states
  • [ ] Below 1024 px, a Menu button opens the links in a native dialog named "Main menu"; Close, Escape, a click that starts and ends on the backdrop, and a followed link close it, and focus returns to Menu
  • [ ] Calls to action that go to a page are links, and each one's accessible name starts with its visible text
  • [ ] Testimonials, logos, and numbers are the user's real content, or placeholders marked as such; nothing is invented
  • [ ] Testimonials are figures with a blockquote and a figcaption; an avatar beside its name has empty alt text, and logos are named after their company
  • [ ] The hero's headline and image are visible at load; the hero image has fetchpriority="high", and every image has width and height
  • [ ] A background video has a visible pause button and doesn't play on its own under reduced motion; a video with speech has captions
  • [ ] Without script, under reduced motion, and when printing, every section is visible; with the scroll reveal, nothing in view is ever hidden, after a reload or Back included, a section fades in once any part of it scrolls into view, and focus shows it at once, mid-fade included
  • [ ] The grids come from CSS alone, nothing scrolls sideways at 320 px wide, and no section hides its overflow
  • [ ] An email signup has a visible label, type="email" with autocomplete="email", and gives its result in the status region
  • [ ] Text meets 4.5:1 and focus indicators 3:1 against every section's background, text over images included
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Navigation Bar (Responsive) with Mobile Menu: the header in full, with its dropdowns and the menu on small screens.
  • Pricing Table: a pricing section with a billing choice.
  • Button: the calls to action's styles and states.
  • Form Validation Pattern: the email signup's errors and timing.
  • Blog Layout (List and Post): a blog that shares the header and the footer.

These are suggestions; the page works on its own.
excerpt: A marketing page from the header to the footer: a header that sticks with CSS alone and turns solid as the page scrolls, calls to action that are links, social proof from the user's real content, and motion that never leaves a section hidden.

title: Ecommerce Product Page
body:
A product page supports one decision: whether to buy this, in this option. Its common mistakes cost both sales and trust: a disabled Add to cart that doesn't say why, sold-out sizes shown only in gray, a sale price read out as two numbers, and a cart request that trusts the browser's price. This guide covers the page from the gallery to the recommendations, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has product page parts, in its storefront, its commerce platform's theme, or a library it already uses, configure or extend them to meet this guide. Keep their APIs.
  2. Otherwise build it from plain HTML: the buy box is a <form> that posts to the cart, with a <fieldset> for each option group.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

The first screen

  • From 1024 px, the gallery (55 to 65% of the width) and the buy box sit side by side, so the shopper can look and buy without scrolling. On phones they stack: the gallery, then the buy box.
  • The buy box holds, in this order: the product's title (the page's <h1>), the rating summary, the price, the options, the quantity, Add to cart, and delivery and returns. Nothing needed to buy is in a tab or an accordion.
  • A sticky buy box on wide screens is optional, and only if it fits the window below the sticky header.

The gallery

  • The main image, and thumbnails as buttons named after their image ("Front view", "Fabric close-up"), the shown one marked with aria-current="true" and by more than color.
  • A "View full size" button opens the full-size view in a native <dialog>, as the Modal Dialog guide says: the rest of the page is inert, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the button. Zoom on hover is an extra, never the only way.
  • Swiping between images needs buttons too (WCAG 2.5.1), and works with them alone.
  • The first image loads at once with fetchpriority="high"; the others loading="lazy". Every image has width and height, or the gallery an aspect-ratio, so nothing shifts.
  • A video doesn't play with sound on its own, has visible controls, and has captions when it has speech.

Price

  • Prices are formatted with Intl.NumberFormat for the currency and the locale, and say whether tax is included where that's required.
  • A compare-at price is struck through, which most screen readers don't announce, so "$58 $48" is unclear. Add visually hidden text: "Was $58, now $48". A saving ("Save 17%") is worked out from the two prices, rounded down.

Options

  • Each group (color, size) is a <fieldset> with a <legend>, and its options are native radios: one Tab stop, and the arrows choose. The chosen value shows beside the legend ("Size: M").
  • Color swatches are radios named after the color ("Navy"), drawn as swatches.
  • An option that can't be bought says so in its label ("M, sold out"), not only with a strike-through or a faded color (WCAG 1.4.1). It can be disabled, which the arrows skip (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit); the words in its label are what say why.
  • When a choice in one group makes the chosen option of another unavailable (a size sold out in the new color), that option is cleared, and the status region says so ("M isn't available in Navy").
  • Price, availability, delivery, and images follow the chosen options. With many options, a select or a combobox (the Select and Combobox guide).

Add to cart

  • Add to cart is never disabled, since a disabled button can't be focused and doesn't say what's missing. Pressed while an option group has no choice it can send, or while the quantity breaks its rules, it sends nothing, shows each problem's message, and moves focus to the first: the group's first option that can be chosen, or the quantity field.
  • Each message sits in its control's description (aria-describedby on the group's fieldset, or on the field), and is empty while it's hidden, so it adds nothing until it shows; the quantity field also has aria-invalid="true" while its message shows. A message goes as soon as its problem is fixed.
  • Without script, required on the radios and the quantity field's own rules make the browser block the post and focus the first problem (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). The script sets novalidate and shows its own messages instead, as the Form Validation Pattern does, so it checks every rule the browser would have: a check of the option groups alone let quantities 0, 6, 1.5, and an empty one reach the cart (checked in all three).
  • The quantity is a required number field with min="1" and a max that follows the stock, so a fraction fails its step; its message says the range ("Enter a quantity from 1 to 5"). Stepper buttons, if any, are named "Decrease quantity" and "Increase quantity".

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<form class="buy-box" id="buy-form" action="/cart" method="post">   <input type="hidden" name="product" value="organic-tee">   <fieldset class="option-group" aria-describedby="size-error" data-error="Choose a size">     <legend>Size</legend>     <p class="field-error" id="size-error" hidden></p>     <label><input type="radio" name="size" value="s" required> S</label>     <label><input type="radio" name="size" value="m" required disabled> M, sold out</label>     <label><input type="radio" name="size" value="l" required> L</label>   </fieldset>   <label for="quantity">Quantity</label>   <input id="quantity" name="quantity" type="number" inputmode="numeric" min="1" max="5" value="1" required     aria-describedby="quantity-error" data-error="Enter a quantity from 1 to 5">   <p class="field-error" id="quantity-error" hidden></p>   <button type="submit">Add to cart</button> </form> <!-- The phone's purchase bar submits the same form, so the same check runs --> <div class="purchase-bar" role="region" aria-label="Quick purchase" hidden>   <button type="submit" form="buy-form">Add to cart</button> </div> 
// Add to cart is never disabled. Pressed while an option group has no choice it can send, or the // quantity breaks its rules, it shows each problem's message, moves focus to the first, and sends // nothing. With novalidate set, this is the only check, so it covers every rule the browser would // have; without script, the browser checks the same rules itself. const form = document.getElementById('buy-form'); const options = (group) => [...group.querySelectorAll('input[type="radio"]')]; // A group needs a choice that can be sent (a chosen option that became unavailable can't be); // any other field, its own rules (required, min, max, step) const invalid = (control) => (control.matches('fieldset')   ? !options(control).some((option) => option.checked && !option.disabled)   : !control.validity.valid); form.noValidate = true;  function setError(control, message) {   const error = document.getElementById(control.getAttribute('aria-describedby'));   error.textContent = message; // empty while hidden, so it adds nothing to the description   error.hidden = !message;   if (!control.matches('input')) return;   if (message) control.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');   else control.removeAttribute('aria-invalid'); } form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {   const controls = [...form.querySelectorAll('[data-error]')];   const problems = controls.filter(invalid);   for (const control of controls) setError(control, problems.includes(control) ? control.dataset.error : '');   if (problems.length === 0) return; // sent as usual   event.preventDefault();   const first = problems[0];   (first.matches('fieldset') ? options(first).find((option) => !option.disabled) : first)?.focus(); }); // A message goes as soon as its problem is fixed form.addEventListener('input', (event) => {   const control = event.target.closest('[data-error]');   if (control && !invalid(control)) setError(control, ''); });

Sending

  • The cart request sends the product, the chosen options, and the quantity, never the price: the server prices the order.
  • While it's out, the button keeps focus with aria-disabled="true" and ignores a second press. The result goes to the page's one polite status region ("Added to your cart: Organic Cotton Tee, M"), the cart's count goes in the cart link's name ("Cart, 2 items"), and a mini cart or a toast is optional.
  • A request that times out may have added the item, so the outcome is unknown, not failed: read the cart again before saying anything, and send a retry with the same request id, so it can't add the item twice.
  • An error that the shopper can fix points to the field it's about, as the missing choice does.

The purchase bar on phones

  • On phones, a purchase bar with the price and Add to cart appears when the buy box's button has left the window: an IntersectionObserver on that button decides, not a scroll handler. While it's not shown, it's hidden (or inert while it animates), not only moved off screen.
  • Its button submits the same form with form="…", so the same check runs (checked: the submit event names it as the submitter in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). It's a region named for its purpose, "Quick purchase".
  • scroll-padding-bottom at its height, with scroll-padding-top at the sticky header's, keeps the focused element clear of both (WCAG 2.2 2.4.11). env(safe-area-inset-bottom) pads it only when the viewport meta tag has viewport-fit=cover.

Details and delivery

  • Delivery, returns, and pickup sit near Add to cart, in plain text that depends on the shopper's region when it differs.
  • Highlights, the description, specifications (a <dl> or a table with row headers), fit or dimensions, materials and care, and questions. On phones, each can be a <details> with its heading in the <summary>; nothing needed to buy is inside one.

Reviews

  • A summary near the title: the stars are images, so the rating is text ("4.8 out of 5 stars, 218 reviews"), and it links to the reviews section.
  • The distribution's bars have their numbers in text ("5 stars: 70%"). Filtering and sorting say how many reviews show, in the status region, as the Data Table guide's filter does.
  • Review text and answers are user content: rendered as text, never as raw HTML. "Verified purchase" is text, not only an icon.
  • With no reviews yet, say so, with a way to write the first.

Recommendations

  • Related products come after the decision content (details and reviews), never before the buy box, shown as the store's usual product cards.
  • A horizontal rail scrolls with the keyboard (its links are in the Tab order) and shows that it scrolls, such as a part of the next card; a hidden scrollbar isn't the only cue.

Structured data

  • If the project manages structured data, render it on the server from the same data as the page: the product, its offers per option with their own prices and availability, and the rating. Don't hardcode prices into it.

Layers

Layers, bottom to top: the page, sticky bars, dropdowns and popovers, toasts, then modals, which make the rest of the page inert. The project's layering scale wins; native <dialog> and the popover attribute use the top layer and need no z-index. The sticky header and the purchase bar are sticky bars, and the full-size gallery is a modal.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • The buy box is 360 to 440 px wide from 1024 px; the title 32 to 44 px (24 to 32 px on phones); the price 28 to 36 px.
  • Text meets 4.5:1, and focus indicators, the chosen option's marker, and form fields' edges 3:1. A message such as "Choose a size" in #b91c1c on white is 6.5:1. Check the project's own colors the same way.
  • Touch targets are at least 44 px, and nothing scrolls sideways at 320 px wide.
  • Motion is optional: images cross-fade over 180 ms, and the purchase bar fades in. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, nothing slides.

Edge cases

  • Sold out entirely: replace Add to cart with a back-in-stock signup, and say "Sold out" in text.
  • Many options: a select or a combobox instead of radios, with the same message and focus on a missing choice.
  • No reviews yet: say so, with a way to write the first.
  • A long title: it wraps; the price and Add to cart stay in the first screen on phones.
  • Delivery depends on the address: say so, and ask for a postcode only when the shopper wants the estimate.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] The product's title is the page's h1, and from 1024 px the gallery and the buy box share the first screen
  • [ ] Gallery thumbnails are buttons named after their image, the shown one is marked, and a button opens the full-size view in a native dialog
  • [ ] The first image loads at once with fetchpriority="high", the others lazily, and every image has width and height
  • [ ] Each option group is a fieldset with a legend and radios, and swatches are named after their color
  • [ ] A sold-out option says so in its label, and a choice that makes another one unavailable clears it and says so
  • [ ] A sale price is read as "Was $58, now $48", and prices are formatted for the locale
  • [ ] Add to cart is never disabled: with a missing choice or a quantity outside its rules, it sends nothing, shows each problem's message, and moves focus to the first
  • [ ] Without script, the radios' required and the quantity's required, min, max, and step make the browser block the post the same way
  • [ ] The cart request sends the product, the options, and the quantity, never the price
  • [ ] Adding says the result in the status region; a timeout reads the cart again instead of saying it failed, and a retry can't add the item twice
  • [ ] The phone's purchase bar is hidden until the buy box's button leaves the window, submits the same form, and never covers the focused element
  • [ ] The rating is text ("4.8 out of 5 stars, 218 reviews"), review text is rendered as text, and filtering reviews says how many show
  • [ ] Nothing scrolls sideways at 320 px wide, and touch targets are at least 44 px
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Modal Dialog: the full-size gallery, as a native dialog.
  • Select and Combobox: groups with many options.
  • Form Validation Pattern: the timing and wording of the missing choice's message.
  • Toast Notifications: a short confirmation after adding to the cart.
  • Tabs Component: the details on wide screens, when they're short.
  • Button: Add to cart and the other actions.

These are suggestions; the page works on its own.
excerpt: A product page whose gallery and buy box share the first screen: options that say when they're sold out, an Add to cart that is never disabled and points to the missing choice, and a cart request the server prices.

title: Documentation Website Layout
body:
Documentation is read in pieces: people arrive from search at one heading, copy one command, and leave. Its layout's common mistakes are a scroll spy that fills the history with headings, a sidebar that covers the footer or traps focus, copy buttons that only appear on hover, and labels cut off with an ellipsis. This guide covers the header and search, the sidebar, the article with its code and callouts, and the table of contents, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project uses a docs framework (Docusaurus, Nextra, VitePress, Starlight, Mintlify) or has a docs layout, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its APIs.
  2. Prefer its search: the framework's own, DocSearch, or Pagefind.
  3. Otherwise build it from plain HTML: a grid with a <header>, a <nav> for the sidebar, <main>, a <nav> for the table of contents, and a <footer>.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

The page grid

  • The page scrolls, not a box inside it. The header sticks to the top, and scroll-padding-top on the root element, set to its height, scrolls focused elements and link targets clear of it (WCAG 2.2 2.4.11); headings need no scroll-margin-top of their own.
  • From 1280 px, three columns: the sidebar (260 px), the content (up to 768 px, in a minmax(0, 1fr) column, so a wide table or code block can't widen the page), and the table of contents (220 px). From 1024 px, two: the sidebar and the content. Below 1024 px, one: the content, with the sidebar as a drawer.
  • The sidebar's column and the table of contents are sticky below the header, as tall as the window minus the header, and scroll inside themselves. A fixed sidebar would cover the start of the footer, which spans the page after the content; a sticky one ends with its column.
  • The header and the footer are as wide as the page (100%), not the viewport's width, which includes the scrollbar on Windows and makes the page scroll sideways.

The header

  • A skip link to <main id="main" tabindex="-1">, the logo, a <nav> labelled "Main" with the site's sections (Docs, API, Blog), the search button, the theme control, and the repository link. Below 1024 px, a Menu button for the drawer.
  • The search button's name is its visible text ("Search docs"). It shows its shortcut as "⌘K" on Apple systems and "Ctrl K" elsewhere, with aria-keyshortcuts="Meta+K Control+K".
  • The theme control follows the Dark/Light Mode guide: a button with aria-pressed for two themes, or a radio group or a menu with light, dark, and system for three. A button that cycles through three themes doesn't say what the next press does.
  • The repository link is named "GitHub"; like any link that opens a new tab, it says so ("GitHub, opens in a new tab").

Search

  • Prefer the project's existing search: the docs framework's own, DocSearch, or Pagefind. Configure it to meet this guide rather than building another.
  • Otherwise: Cmd+K or Ctrl+K, or the search button, opens a modal dialog with a search field and a list of results, with the APG combobox's keys; Escape closes it, and focus returns to the button. The number of results goes to a polite status region once typing pauses. The Command Palette guide covers it in full.

The sidebar

  • One <nav> labelled "Docs", with lists of links. A group is a disclosure: a button with aria-expanded that shows its list; a closed list is hidden, so its links aren't in the Tab order. The Sidebar Navigation guide covers it in full.
  • The current page's group is open on load, from the URL on the server, and its link has aria-current="page" and looks different by more than color. The current link is scrolled into view in the sidebar on load.
  • Saving which other groups are open is optional; if saved, it applies before the first paint, under the app's own prefix (such as acme.docs.groups), or the sidebar jumps after hydration.
  • Links wrap; nothing is cut off with an ellipsis. Tab moves through the links; arrow keys between them are an optional extra, as in the APG disclosure navigation example.

The drawer on small screens

  • Below 1024 px, the Menu button (aria-expanded, aria-controls) opens the same <nav> as a drawer over the page. There's no second copy, so no id appears twice.
  • While it's open, everything else is inert (the Modal Dialog guide's model, without a focus-trap library), so focus and screen readers stay in it, and the page behind doesn't scroll. Focus moves to its Close button ("Close menu"); Close, Escape, a click on the backdrop, and a followed link close it, and focus returns to Menu.
  • When the window crosses 1024 px, focus on an element that hides moves to the nearest control that stays: from Menu or Close to the current page's link, from the sidebar to Menu. React to a matchMedia change, not to resize events. The Dashboard guide's drawer snippet does all of this.

The article

  • Breadcrumbs, when the docs have levels: a <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> with an ordered list, the current page last with aria-current="page", and the separators hidden from screen readers.
  • The page's title is its only <h1>. Text is 16 px at line height 1.7, at most 768 px wide; links in the text are underlined.
  • Headings <h2> and <h3> have ids. A heading's anchor link comes after the heading, not inside it, so it doesn't join the heading's name; it's named after it ("Link to Installation"), and shows on focus as well as on hover.
  • Callouts have a text label ("Note", "Warning", "Danger"), visible or visually hidden, besides their color and icon (WCAG 1.4.1).
  • Variants of the same code (npm, pnpm, yarn) are tabs, as in the Tabs guide.
  • "Last updated" is a <time datetime>; "Edit this page" says so when it opens a new tab. Previous and next pages are links in a <nav aria-label="Pages">, each with its direction and the page's title in its text.

Code blocks

  • A code block is a <figure>; its file name, if any, is the <figcaption>. A block that scrolls sideways gets tabindex="0", so the keyboard can scroll it, and the page itself never scrolls sideways.
  • Copy copies the code's text and reads "Copied" for a moment; the page's one status region says it too, emptied first, so a second copy is announced again. The clipboard can refuse: navigator.clipboard.writeText was refused in Chromium without the clipboard permission and allowed after a click in Firefox and WebKit (checked). Then Copy says so and selects the code, so the keyboard's copy shortcut works.
  • Line numbers are drawn with CSS counters, or left out of what Copy copies, so screen readers and the clipboard get only the code. Highlighting happens at build time, and every token color meets 4.5:1 against the block's background.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version. The drawer is the Dashboard guide's drawer snippet, and the sidebar's groups are in the Sidebar Navigation guide.

<figure class="code-block">   <figcaption>app/layout.tsx</figcaption>   <button type="button" class="code-copy">Copy</button>   <!-- tabindex="0" lets the keyboard scroll a block that's wider than the column -->   <pre tabindex="0"><code>export default function Layout({ children }) {   return <main id="main">{children}</main>; }</code></pre> </figure> <!-- once per page, in the page from the start --> <p class="visually-hidden" role="status" id="page-status"></p> 
// Copy copies the code's text and reads "Copied" for a moment, and the page's status region says // it too, emptied first so a second copy is announced again. If the clipboard refuses, it says // so and selects the code, so the keyboard's copy shortcut works. const status = document.getElementById('page-status');  function say(message) {   status.textContent = '';   setTimeout(() => { status.textContent = message; }, 100); } for (const button of document.querySelectorAll('.code-copy')) {   const code = button.closest('.code-block').querySelector('code');   let reset;   button.addEventListener('click', async () => {     try {       await navigator.clipboard.writeText(code.textContent);       button.textContent = 'Copied';       say('Copied');     } catch {       getSelection().selectAllChildren(code);       say("Couldn't copy. The code is selected, so you can copy it yourself.");     }     clearTimeout(reset);     reset = setTimeout(() => { button.textContent = 'Copy'; }, 2000);   }); }

The table of contents

  • From 1280 px the table of contents is its own column: a <nav> labelled by its heading, "On this page", with links to the page's <h2> and <h3>, sticky below the header and scrolling inside itself. Below 1280 px the same list sits in a collapsed <details> with the summary "On this page" at the top of the content. With fewer than two headings, leave it out.
  • The scroll spy marks the link of the section being read with aria-current="true", and never touches the URL. Setting the URL's hash on every change adds a history entry for each heading and jumps the page, so Back walks through headings; history.replaceState adds none (both checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). A click on a link of the table of contents is a normal link, with one history entry.
  • A heading counts once its top passes a line that follows the scroll down to 30% of the window; over the last window of scrolling, the line moves on to the bottom. A fixed band (such as an IntersectionObserver with a root margin of 60 px at the top and 70% at the bottom) misses the first heading, which starts above it, and the last headings of a page whose last sections are short, which never reach it: in a 700 px window, only the second of four headings ever entered it (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit).
<nav class="toc" aria-labelledby="toc-title">   <h2 id="toc-title">On this page</h2>   <ul>     <li><a href="#install">Install</a></li>     <li>       <a href="#configure">Configure</a>       <ul>         <li><a href="#options">Options</a></li>       </ul>     </li>     <li><a href="#deploy">Deploy</a></li>   </ul> </nav> 
// Marks the table of contents' link for the section being read, and never touches the URL. A // heading counts once its top passes a line that follows the scroll down to 30% of the window; // over the last window of scrolling, the line moves on to the bottom, so the short sections at // the end get their turn. At the very top, and on a page that doesn't scroll, the first counts. const links = [...document.querySelectorAll('.toc a[href^="#"]')]; const headings = [...new Set(links.map((link) => decodeURIComponent(link.hash.slice(1))))]   .map((id) => document.getElementById(id))   .filter(Boolean); let frame = 0;  function update() {   frame = 0;   const end = document.documentElement.scrollHeight - innerHeight;   const start = Math.max(0, end - innerHeight);   const top = Math.min(scrollY, innerHeight * 0.3);   const toEnd = end > start ? Math.min(1, Math.max(0, (scrollY - start) / (end - start))) : 0;   const line = top + (innerHeight - top) * toEnd;   const current = headings.findLast((heading) => heading.getBoundingClientRect().top <= line) ?? headings[0];   for (const link of links) {     if (current && decodeURIComponent(link.hash.slice(1)) === current.id) link.setAttribute('aria-current', 'true');     else link.removeAttribute('aria-current');   } } const schedule = () => { frame ||= requestAnimationFrame(update); }; addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true }); addEventListener('resize', schedule); update();

Route changes

  • In a single-page app, a route change updates document.title, moves focus to the new page's <h1> (tabindex="-1") unless the framework announces routes itself, closes the drawer, moves aria-current, and starts the scroll spy on the new headings.

Versions

  • A version switcher is a disclosure with links, as the Navigation Bar guide's dropdowns are. A <select> that navigates when its value changes changes the context on input (WCAG 3.2.2).

Layers

Layers, bottom to top: the page, sticky bars, dropdowns and popovers, toasts, then modals, which make the rest of the page inert. The project's layering scale wins; native <dialog> and the popover attribute use the top layer and need no z-index. The header, the sidebar's column, and the table of contents are sticky bars, and the drawer and the search dialog are modals.

Phones and right-to-left text

  • Logical properties (inset-inline-start, margin-inline-end) put the sidebar on the start side and the table of contents on the end side in right-to-left text.
  • On phones with a notch, env(safe-area-inset-top) pads the header only when the viewport meta tag has viewport-fit=cover.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • The header is 60 px tall; the sidebar 260 px, the content up to 768 px, the table of contents 220 px; content padding 32 to 48 px, and 16 to 20 px on phones.
  • Light: #ffffff with #1f2937 text (14.7:1), #6b7280 muted text (4.8:1), and #4f46e5 for links and the current section (6.3:1); #6366f1 is only 4.47:1. Dark: #0a0a0a with #d4d4d8 text (13.4:1), #a1a1aa muted text (7.7:1), #fafafa headings (19.0:1), and #818cf8 for links and the current section (6.6:1); #71717a is only 4.1:1.
  • Callouts: a tinted background with a dark label, #1d4ed8 on #eff6ff for a note (6.2:1), #92400e on #fffbeb for a warning (6.8:1), and #991b1b on #fef2f2 for danger (7.6:1).
  • Motion is optional: the drawer slides in over 300 ms, and links to headings scroll smoothly only under prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference; under reduce, nothing slides.

Edge cases

  • A short page: with fewer than two headings, the table of contents is left out and the content takes its space.
  • A long sidebar: it scrolls inside itself, with the current link scrolled into view on load.
  • Deep nesting: three levels at most in the sidebar; past that, split the section.
  • Printing: hide the header's links, the sidebar, and the table of contents, and let code wrap.
  • Before the script runs: from 1024 px the sidebar works without it; below, the drawer needs it, so keep the docs reachable without it too, such as from the docs' home page.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] The page starts with a skip link, and the header, the sidebar, the main area, the table of contents, and the footer are landmarks; the two navs have different names
  • [ ] The page scrolls, the header sticks, scroll-padding-top keeps a focused link clear of it, and nothing scrolls sideways at 320 px wide
  • [ ] From 1024 px the sidebar is a sticky column; below, Menu opens the same nav as a drawer with a Close button, and the rest of the page is inert
  • [ ] Close, Escape, the backdrop, and a followed link close the drawer, focus returns to Menu, and crossing 1024 px keeps focus on something that shows
  • [ ] The sidebar's groups are disclosure buttons, the current page's group is open on load, and its link has aria-current="page"
  • [ ] The search button is named by its visible text and opens search with Cmd+K on Apple systems and Ctrl+K elsewhere
  • [ ] From 1280 px the table of contents is a sticky column; below, a collapsed "On this page" disclosure at the top of the content; it is left out with fewer than two headings
  • [ ] Scrolling marks the section being read, the last short sections included, adds no history entries, and leaves the URL alone
  • [ ] Each heading's anchor link comes after the heading, is named after it, and shows on focus as well as on hover
  • [ ] Copy copies the code and says "Copied", or says that copying failed and selects the code; a second copy is announced too
  • [ ] A code block that scrolls sideways can be reached with Tab, and line numbers are not part of what Copy copies
  • [ ] Callouts have a text label, such as "Warning", besides their color and icon
  • [ ] Links in the article are underlined, and text meets 4.5:1 in both themes
  • [ ] In a single-page app, a route change updates the title, moves focus to the new page's h1, and closes the drawer
  • [ ] Under reduced motion nothing slides, and links to headings jump instead of scrolling smoothly
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Command Palette: the search dialog in full, opened with Cmd or Ctrl+K.
  • Sidebar Navigation: the sidebar's groups in full.
  • Dashboard Layout with Collapsible Sidebar: the drawer snippet, with the rest of the page inert and focus kept across 1024 px.
  • Navigation Bar (Responsive) with Mobile Menu: the header's links and its dropdowns, such as a version switcher.
  • Tabs Component: variants of the same code, such as npm, pnpm, and yarn.
  • Dark/Light Mode: the theme control and a theme set before the first paint.
  • Button: Copy, Menu, and the header's buttons.

These are suggestions; the layout works on its own.

title: Dashboard Layout with Collapsible Sidebar
body:
A dashboard's shell holds everything else: the sidebar, the header with search and the account menu, and the tables and charts in between. The shell's own mistakes are about space and focus: fixed bars that cover what has focus, a content box that scrolls on its own, a wide table that pushes the page sideways, and a mobile sidebar whose page stays reachable behind it. This guide covers the shell, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA; the Sidebar Navigation guide covers the sidebar itself.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has an app shell or layout components, in its design system or a framework it already uses, configure or extend them to meet this guide. Keep their APIs.
  2. Otherwise build it from plain HTML: a grid with a <nav>, a <header>, <main>, and a <footer>.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

The page grid

  • The page scrolls, not a box inside it. A grid has two columns: the sidebar's, sticky at the top at the window's full height and scrolling inside itself, and the main column, whose header is sticky at its top. The footer sits at the end of the main area and scrolls with the content; it's never fixed. Keyboard scrolling then works without first focusing an area, and so do find in page, links to a section, the scroll position after Back, and phone toolbars that hide while scrolling.
  • scroll-padding-top on the root element, set to the header's height, makes the page scroll focused elements and link targets clear of the header (WCAG 2.2 2.4.11). Checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit: with it, a link focused under the header is scrolled clear (Chromium and Firefox center it, WebKit puts it just below the header); without it, the link stays covered.
  • The main column is minmax(0, 1fr). Grid and flex children default to min-width: auto, so with 1fr a table with many columns or a long line of code widens the page, even inside its own scrolling container (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). Wide tables and code blocks scroll inside their own container, as the Data Table guide says; don't hide overflow on the content area, which clips content and focus outlines.
  • Full heights use 100dvh, with 100vh before it for older browsers, so phone toolbars don't hide the bottom.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version. The sidebar's own markup, its collapsed rail, and its saved state are in the Sidebar Navigation guide.

<a class="skip-link" href="#main">Skip to content</a> <div class="app">   <nav class="sidebar" id="sidebar" aria-label="Main">     <button type="button" class="drawer-close">Close menu</button>     <!-- the sidebar's links (the Sidebar Navigation guide) -->   </nav>   <div class="drawer-backdrop" hidden></div>   <div class="app-main">     <header class="app-header">       <button type="button" class="menu-button" aria-controls="sidebar" aria-expanded="false">Menu</button>       <!-- search, notifications, the account menu -->     </header>     <main id="main" tabindex="-1">       <h1>Orders</h1>       <!-- the page -->     </main>     <footer class="app-footer">       <!-- scrolls with the page, never fixed -->     </footer>   </div> </div> 
/* The page scrolls. The sidebar's column and the header stick, and the page scrolls focused    elements and link targets clear of the header. */ .app {   display: grid;   grid-template-columns: auto minmax(0, 1fr); /* minmax: wide content can't widen the page */   min-height: 100vh;   min-height: 100dvh; } .sidebar {   align-self: start;   height: 100vh;   height: 100dvh;   overflow-y: auto;   position: sticky;   top: 0; } .app-header {   min-height: 64px;   position: sticky;   top: 0;   z-index: 10; /* the sticky-bar layer of the project's scale */ } html {   scroll-padding-top: 64px; /* the header's height */ }

Landmarks and headings

  • The sidebar comes first in the page, so the page starts with a skip link to <main id="main" tabindex="-1"> (WCAG 2.4.1).
  • The sidebar is a labelled <nav>, the header a <header>, the content <main>, and the footer a <footer>.
  • The page's title is its <h1>, at the start of <main>. Breadcrumbs, when the app has them, are a <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> with an ordered list, the current page last with aria-current="page", and the separators hidden from screen readers.
  • In a single-page app, a route change updates document.title, moves focus to the new page's <h1> (tabindex="-1"), closes the drawer and any open menu, and moves aria-current.

The sidebar

  • It's the Sidebar Navigation guide's sidebar: 260 px expanded and 64 px collapsed as suggested defaults, with an 80 px rail with a short label under each icon as an option. In the rail, labels are hidden visually only, so every link keeps its name, and the collapse toggle's name says what it does ("Collapse sidebar", "Expand sidebar").
  • A saved collapsed state is applied before the first paint, by a cookie the server reads or a small inline script, and stored under the app's own prefix, such as acme.sidebar. The rail's styles apply from 1024 px only, so a saved rail never shrinks the drawer.
  • Collapsing changes the main column's width. Charts and virtualized tables measure their container, so they measure again after the change (a ResizeObserver). Under reduced motion, the width changes at once.

The drawer on small screens

  • Below 1024 px, tablets included, a Menu button in the header (aria-expanded, aria-controls) opens the same sidebar as a drawer over the page. There's no second copy, so no id appears twice.
  • While it's open, everything else is inert (the Modal Dialog guide's model, without a focus-trap library), so focus and screen readers stay in it, and the page behind doesn't scroll. It makes inert only what isn't inert yet, and closing undoes only that, so a part of the page the app made inert stays inert. Focus moves to its Close button.
  • Close ("Close menu"), Escape, a click on the backdrop, and a followed link close it, and focus returns to Menu.
  • If the window gets wider than 1024 px while it's open, it docks, and the inertness it added goes.
  • When the window crosses 1024 px, focus on an element that hides moves to the nearest control that stays, and focus anywhere else stays where it is. Widening hides Menu and Close, so focus on them, the drawer open or closed, moves to the current page's link, or to the first link that shows when that one is in a closed group (a selector list such as [aria-current="page"], a finds whichever comes first in the page, so pick the current one first); narrowing hides the docked sidebar, so focus in it moves to Menu. The same goes for any header control the project hides at a breakpoint. Chromium drops focus from an element a media query hides before a matchMedia listener runs, so the snippet remembers the last focused element and checks whether it still shows. React to a matchMedia change, not to resize events.
/* Below 1024 px the same sidebar is a drawer over the page */ @media (max-width: 1023.98px) {   .app {     grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr);   }   .sidebar {     height: auto;     inset-block: 0;     inset-inline-start: 0;     position: fixed;     width: min(260px, 85vw);     z-index: 30; /* the modal layer of the project's scale */   }   .sidebar:not(.is-open) {     display: none;   }   .drawer-backdrop {     background: rgb(0 0 0 / 50%);     inset: 0;     position: fixed;     z-index: 29;   }   html:has(.sidebar.is-open) {     overflow: hidden; /* the page behind doesn't scroll */   } } @media (min-width: 1024px) {   .menu-button,   .drawer-close {     display: none;   } } 
// Below 1024 px the sidebar is a drawer. While it's open, everything else is inert, so focus // and screen readers stay in it; Close, Escape, and a click on the backdrop close it. const sidebar = document.getElementById('sidebar'); const menuButton = document.querySelector('.menu-button'); const closeButton = sidebar.querySelector('.drawer-close'); const backdrop = document.querySelector('.drawer-backdrop'); const wide = matchMedia('(min-width: 1024px)'); let madeInert = []; // closing undoes only this, so what was inert before stays inert let lastFocused = null;  function setOpen(open) {   sidebar.classList.toggle('is-open', open);   backdrop.hidden = !open;   menuButton.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(open));   madeInert.forEach((element) => { element.inert = false; });   madeInert = [];   if (!open) return;   for (let node = sidebar; node !== document.body; node = node.parentElement) {     for (const sibling of node.parentElement.children) {       if (sibling !== node && sibling !== backdrop && !sibling.inert) madeInert.push(sibling);     }   }   madeInert.forEach((element) => { element.inert = true; }); } function close() {   setOpen(false);   menuButton.focus(); } menuButton.addEventListener('click', () => {   setOpen(true);   closeButton.focus(); }); closeButton.addEventListener('click', close); backdrop.addEventListener('click', close); sidebar.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {   if (event.key === 'Escape' && sidebar.classList.contains('is-open')) close(); }); // Crossing 1024 px moves the same sidebar between the drawer and its column, and hides Menu and // Close, or the sidebar. Focus on what hides moves to what stays: to the current page's link when // the sidebar docks (or the first link that shows, when that one is in a closed group), to Menu // when it hides; focus anywhere else stays where it is. Chromium drops that focus before this // runs, so the last focused element says where it was. const shownLink = () => [...sidebar.querySelectorAll('a[aria-current="page"]'), ...sidebar.querySelectorAll('a[href]')]   .find((link) => link.checkVisibility()); document.addEventListener('focusin', (event) => { lastFocused = event.target; }); wide.addEventListener('change', () => {   const lost = !document.activeElement || document.activeElement === document.body;   const focused = lost ? lastFocused : document.activeElement;   if (wide.matches) setOpen(false);   if (!focused?.isConnected || focused.checkVisibility()) return;   if (wide.matches) shownLink()?.focus();   else menuButton.focus(); });

The header

  • The header holds the Menu button below 1024 px, then search or the command palette's trigger, notifications, and the account menu.
  • The account menu is a disclosure, as in the Navigation Bar guide: a button with aria-expanded, and a list of links. Sign out is a button that posts a form. It isn't role="menu", which promises arrow-key navigation, and no button here has aria-haspopup.
  • The notifications button's name includes the count ("Notifications, 3 unread"); the badge is hidden from screen readers, and its panel is a disclosure too.
  • Escape closes an open menu or panel and puts focus back on its button; a click outside closes it.
  • Nothing announces "Sidebar opened": the Menu button's aria-expanded already says it.

Live content

  • Widgets that refresh don't announce themselves, and the dashboard's grid isn't a live region. One polite status region, in the page from the start, says the results people asked for ("Report exported"); role="alert" is only for urgent errors.
  • Each widget keeps its own loading, empty, and error states, as the Data Table guide does for tables, so each still works on its own.

Layers

Layers, bottom to top: the page, sticky bars, dropdowns and popovers, toasts, then modals, which make the rest of the page inert. The project's layering scale wins; native <dialog> and the popover attribute use the top layer and need no z-index. The sticky header and the sidebar's column are sticky bars, the header's panels are dropdowns, and the drawer is a modal.

Phones and right-to-left text

  • On phones with a notch, env(safe-area-inset-top) pads the header and the drawer, but only when the viewport meta tag has viewport-fit=cover; without it, the values are 0.
  • Logical properties (inset-inline-start, margin-inline-start) put the sidebar on the start side in right-to-left text, and the drawer slides in from there.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • The header is 64 px tall. Content padding is 24 to 32 px from 1024 px and 16 px on phones; a maximum width for reading, such as 1400 px, is optional.
  • Text meets 4.5:1, and focus indicators, the current link's marker, and form controls' edges 3:1. Check the project's own colors the same way.
  • Motion is optional: the sidebar's width changes over 200 ms, and the drawer slides in over 250 ms. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, nothing slides.
  • Colors: a #f9fafb page with #111827 text (17.0:1), a #ffffff header with #4b5563 icons (7.6:1), and a #111827 sidebar with #d1d5db links (12.0:1) and a #60a5fa marker for the current one (7.0:1). In dark mode, a #030712 page with #f3f4f6 text (18.3:1) and a #1f2937 header and sidebar. A badge with white text needs #dc2626 (4.8:1); #ef4444 is only 3.8:1.

Edge cases

  • Many navigation items: the sidebar's column scrolls on its own, and keeps the current link in view.
  • Short screens: phones in landscape and 400% zoom leave little height, so only the 64 px header sticks; the footer scrolls with the content.
  • Wide content: tables and code scroll inside their own container, and the page doesn't scroll sideways at 320 px wide.
  • A second panel: a panel of filters or details on the other side follows the same rules: its own column from 1024 px, a drawer below.
  • Before the script runs: render the sidebar and the page on the server. Below 1024 px the drawer needs the script, so keep the main sections reachable without it too, such as from the home page.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] The page itself scrolls; the sidebar's column and the header stick, and the footer scrolls with the content
  • [ ] A link focused under the sticky header is scrolled clear of it (scroll-padding-top at the header's height)
  • [ ] A table or code block wider than the column scrolls inside itself, and the page never scrolls sideways, down to 320 px wide
  • [ ] The page starts with a skip link to the main area, and has one h1, the page's title, at the start of main
  • [ ] Breadcrumbs, if any, are a nav named "Breadcrumb" with the current page last, marked aria-current="page"
  • [ ] Below 1024 px, Menu opens the same sidebar as a drawer with a visible Close button, and focus moves into it
  • [ ] While the drawer is open, the rest of the page is inert and doesn't scroll; Close, Escape, the backdrop, and a followed link close it, focus returns to Menu, and what was inert before it opened stays inert
  • [ ] Crossing 1024 px either way, focus on what hides moves to what stays: from Menu or Close to the current page's link (or the first link that shows, when that one is in a closed group), and from the sidebar to Menu; focus anywhere else stays where it is
  • [ ] The account menu and the notifications panel are disclosures that close on Escape and on a click outside; Sign out is a button
  • [ ] The notifications button's name includes the count, and widgets, badges, and the dashboard's grid aren't live regions
  • [ ] In a single-page app, a route change updates the title and moves focus to the new page's h1
  • [ ] A saved collapsed sidebar applies before the first paint, so the layout doesn't shift on load, and from 1024 px only, so the drawer stays expanded
  • [ ] Under reduced motion, the sidebar and the drawer change without sliding
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Sidebar Navigation: the sidebar itself, with its collapsed rail and its saved state.
  • Navigation Bar (Responsive) with Mobile Menu: the same disclosure menus and skip link in a top bar.
  • Command Palette: keyboard-first navigation and commands for dense apps.
  • Data Table (Sortable, Paginated, Filterable): tables in the main area.
  • Modal Dialog: confirmations and forms over the dashboard.
  • Toast Notifications: brief messages about results.
  • Select and Combobox: filters and settings.
  • File Upload Component: imports and attachments.
  • Button: the header's and the page's actions.

These are suggestions; the layout works with any content.
excerpt: An app shell where the page itself scrolls: a sticky header that never covers the focused element, the sidebar in its own column or as a drawer on small screens, and a footer that scrolls with the content.

title: Blog Layout (List and Post)
body:
A blog has two pages, the list and the post, which share a header and a footer. On the list page, the common mistakes are cards that read as one long link and pagination that nobody can tell apart; on the post page, links lost in the text, code that pushes the page sideways, and share buttons that bring in trackers. This guide covers both pages, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has blog templates or a theme, in its CMS, its static site generator, or a library it already uses, configure or extend them to meet this guide. Keep their APIs.
  2. Otherwise build them from plain HTML: <main>, an <article> for the post, an <aside> for the sidebar, and a <nav> for the pagination.
  3. The colors, type, and shapes under "Appearance" are a fallback for a project without a design of its own.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

The two pages

  • The list page: the header, an optional hero with the blog's title, the post cards, an optional sidebar, the pagination, and the footer. The blog's title is the page's <h1>, and each card's title an <h2>.
  • The post page: the header, the post in an <article> (its title as the page's <h1>, the author, the date, the reading time, and an optional image), share links, comments, related posts, and the footer. Comments and related posts are sections with an <h2>, and a related post's card title is an <h3>.
  • Both pages share the header and the footer, start with a skip link to <main id="main" tabindex="-1">, and put an optional sidebar in an <aside> named by its heading.

The header

  • The site's header: a skip link, the logo, a <nav> labelled "Main", and the links that apply (Search, Subscribe). If it sticks, position: sticky and scroll-padding-top at its height keep focused elements clear of it (WCAG 2.2 2.4.11).
  • Below 1024 px, the links move into a menu in a native <dialog>, as the Navigation Bar guide says.

Post cards

  • The card's title link covers the whole card, so a click anywhere follows it, while the card stays one link named by its title. Making the whole card an <a> would read the card's text as the link's name, and the category and author links inside it would be nested links.
  • Other links in the card (a category, an author) sit above the cover, and still work (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). The trade-off: the excerpt's text can't be selected.
  • The image is decorative (alt=""), since the title names the link. Images in the first screen load at once, the featured one with fetchpriority="high"; the rest can be loading="lazy". Every image has width and height.
  • Titles wrap; nothing is cut off with an ellipsis. An excerpt may be clamped to two or three lines, since the post is a click away.
  • The date is a <time datetime="2026-10-01">, and the meta line reads in a sensible order: category, date, reading time.
  • The focus ring goes around the whole card, and a hover changes the shadow; under reduced motion, cards don't move.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<article class="post-card">   <img src="/images/grid-layouts.jpg" alt="" width="640" height="360">   <h2 class="post-card-title"><a href="/posts/grid-layouts">Grid layouts that survive real content</a></h2>   <p>Why minmax(0, 1fr) matters, and three layouts that hold up with long words and wide tables.</p>   <p class="post-card-meta">     <a class="post-card-category" href="/categories/css">CSS</a>     <time datetime="2026-10-01">1 October 2026</time>   </p> </article> 
/* The title's link covers the whole card, so a click anywhere on it follows the link, while the    card stays one link named by its title. Other links in the card sit above the cover. */ .post-card {   position: relative; } .post-card-title a::after {   content: "";   inset: 0;   position: absolute; } .post-card-category {   position: relative;   z-index: 1; } /* The focus ring goes around the whole card */ .post-card-title a:focus-visible {   outline: none; } .post-card-title a:focus-visible::after {   outline: 2px solid currentColor;   outline-offset: 4px; }

The article

  • The body is 16 to 18 px with a line height of 1.6 to 1.8, at most about 70 characters a line (720 px). Headings go <h2> to <h4> in order.
  • Links in the text are underlined. Without an underline, a link's color needs 3:1 against the text around it and another cue on hover and focus (WCAG 1.4.1); the safe default is the underline.
  • Images have alt text that says what they show; an image with a caption is a <figure> with a <figcaption>.
  • A code block scrolls sideways inside itself, never the page. A block that scrolls gets tabindex="0", so the keyboard can scroll it, and sits in a <figure> whose caption names it, as the Documentation guide shows.
  • A post has a table of contents only if it's long; the Documentation guide covers one that marks the section being read.

The sidebar

  • On the list page: categories, tags, search, and the newsletter. Search is a labelled field in a <search> element (or a form with role="search"), so it's a landmark. On the post page: the table of contents, the author's bio, and related posts.
  • Sticky is optional, and only if the sidebar fits the window below the sticky header; otherwise it scrolls inside itself (max-height the window's height minus the header's, overflow-y: auto), or its end can't be reached until the page ends.
  • From 1024 px it sits beside the posts, 280 to 320 px wide; below that it follows the content.

Pagination

  • A <nav aria-label="Pagination"> with a list of links. The current page is marked with aria-current="page" and looks different by more than color.
  • Links can't be disabled, so there's no Previous link on the first page and no Next link on the last; show nothing, or plain text.
  • A page number's name includes the number it shows: "Page", visually hidden, then "2". On phones, Previous, "Page 2 of 8", and Next are enough.
  • Each page has its own URL (/blog/page/2 or ?page=2), so pages can be shared and Back works.

Sharing

  • Share links are plain links to each site's share page (X, LinkedIn, Facebook, Mastodon), without the sites' scripts, which track readers. Each is named "Share on X", and says so when it opens a new tab.
  • Copy link copies the post's canonical address, not the one with tracking parameters. It says "Link copied" on the button for a moment and in the page's one status region, which is emptied first, so a second copy is announced too. The clipboard can refuse: navigator.clipboard.writeText was refused in Chromium without the clipboard permission and allowed after a click in Firefox and WebKit (checked), so a failure is said too.
  • navigator.share() opens the device's share sheet where it exists; feature-detect it, and keep the links for everyone else.
<button type="button" class="copy-link">Copy link</button> <!-- once per page, in the page from the start --> <p class="visually-hidden" role="status" id="page-status"></p> 
// Copies the post's address and says so: on the button for a moment, and in the page's status // region, which is emptied first, so copying again is announced again. The clipboard can refuse, // so a failure is said too. const button = document.querySelector('.copy-link'); const status = document.getElementById('page-status'); const label = button.textContent; let reset;  function say(message) {   status.textContent = '';   setTimeout(() => { status.textContent = message; }, 100); } button.addEventListener('click', async () => {   const url = document.querySelector('link[rel="canonical"]')?.href ?? location.href;   try {     await navigator.clipboard.writeText(url);     button.textContent = 'Link copied';     say('Link copied');   } catch {     say("Couldn't copy the link. Copy it from the address bar.");   }   clearTimeout(reset);   reset = setTimeout(() => { button.textContent = label; }, 2000); });

Comments

  • Comments are user content: render them as text, or as HTML sanitized on the server, never as raw HTML. The server handles spam and moderation.
  • The form's fields have visible labels: name (autocomplete="name"), email (type="email", autocomplete="email"), and the comment. Errors and timing follow the Form Validation Pattern, and the result goes to the status region.
  • An embedded comment service loads third-party scripts and tracking; say so, and ask before adding one.

Newsletter

  • The form says what people sign up for and how often they'll hear from you. The field has a visible label, type="email", and autocomplete="email"; the result ("Check your inbox to confirm") and errors go to the status region.

Motion

  • All motion is optional. The hero and the first cards are visible at load; they don't fade in from opacity 0, which would delay the largest image's paint.
  • A scroll reveal, if any, hides only cards below the window when the script runs, on screens, when motion is allowed, as the Landing Page guide's does. Without script, under reduced motion, and when printing, nothing is hidden.
  • Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, card hovers change color or shadow only.

Layers

Layers, bottom to top: the page, sticky bars, dropdowns and popovers, toasts, then modals, which make the rest of the page inert. The project's layering scale wins; native <dialog> and the popover attribute use the top layer and need no z-index. A sticky header is a sticky bar, and the menu is a modal.

Layout

  • One column of cards below 768 px, two from 768 px; from 1024 px, two beside a sidebar, or three without one, since three beside a 320 px sidebar leaves cards about 240 px wide.
  • The post's header can span the page's width; the body stays at its reading width.
  • At 320 px wide nothing scrolls sideways.

Appearance

  • These values are a fallback for a project without a design of its own; the project's styles, tokens, and components win.
  • Colors: a #ffffff page (or #f8fafc), #0f172a text (17.9:1 on white), #334155 for secondary text (10.4:1), and #475569 for muted text (7.6:1, and 7.2:1 on #f8fafc). Links take the text color and an underline. The accent is neutral: buttons in #0f172a with #ffffff text (17.9:1), and a #0f172a focus ring, 2 px at a 2 px offset. #e2e8f0 is for dividers and card edges only; a form field's edge needs 3:1, such as #64748b (4.8:1).
  • Type: the project's font stack; the post title clamp(2rem, 4vw, 3.25rem) at line height 1.15 to 1.3, card titles 18 to 22 px, the body 18 px at line height 1.7.
  • Shape: cards with a 12 px radius, a #e2e8f0 edge, and the shadow 0 1px 3px rgb(15 23 42 / 8%), raised to 0 8px 24px rgb(15 23 42 / 12%) on hover; buttons and fields with an 8 px radius.
  • Spacing: 48 to 72 px between sections of the list page, 40 to 64 px in the post, and 20 to 28 px inside cards.

Edge cases

  • A post without an image: the card keeps the same title, excerpt, and meta; leave the image's space out rather than showing an empty box.
  • A long title: it wraps on every screen; nothing is cut off.
  • The first and last pages: no Previous link on the first page and no Next link on the last.
  • No comments yet: say so in a sentence, with the form below it.
  • Before the script runs: every card is visible and every link works; only Copy link and the share sheet need the script.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] The list page and the post page each start with a skip link and have one h1; the post is an article, the sidebar an aside, and the pagination a nav
  • [ ] A post card is one link, its title, which covers the whole card; a category or author link inside it still works, and the focus ring goes around the card
  • [ ] Card images are decorative (alt="") when the title names the link; images in the first screen load at once, and every image has width and height
  • [ ] Card titles wrap instead of being cut off; only an excerpt may be clamped
  • [ ] Links in the article's text are underlined, and text meets 4.5:1
  • [ ] A code block scrolls sideways inside itself and can be reached with Tab, and the page never scrolls sideways at 320 px wide
  • [ ] Dates are time elements with a datetime attribute
  • [ ] Pagination marks the current page with aria-current="page", and has no Previous link on the first page or Next link on the last
