  • [ ] Share links go to each site's share page without third-party scripts, and say so when they open a new tab
  • [ ] Copy link copies the post's address and says so in the status region, or says that copying failed; a second copy is announced too
  • [ ] Comments are rendered as text or sanitized HTML, never as raw HTML
  • [ ] The newsletter and comment forms have visible labels, and their results go to the status region
  • [ ] A sticky sidebar fits the window below the header, or scrolls inside itself
  • [ ] Without script, under reduced motion, and when printing, nothing is hidden, and cards don't move on hover under reduced motion
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens; the guide's colors are only a fallback

See also

  • Navigation Bar (Responsive) with Mobile Menu: the header and its menu on small screens.
  • Landing Page Layout (Marketing): a landing page that shares the header, the footer, and the scroll reveal.
  • Documentation Website Layout: code blocks with Copy, and a table of contents that marks the section being read.
  • Text Input Field: the search, newsletter, and comment fields.
  • Form Validation Pattern: errors and timing in the newsletter and comment forms.
  • Button: Copy link, Subscribe, and the forms' buttons.

These are suggestions; the blog works on its own.
excerpt: A blog's list page and post page: post cards whose title link covers the card, an article with underlined links and code that scrolls inside itself, pagination that marks the current page, and sharing without third-party scripts.

title: AI Agent Chat Layout
body:
People talk to an AI assistant through parts every chat shares: a list of conversations, the transcript, and a box to type in. This guide covers that shell. It builds on the chat components your project already has, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA. What goes inside an assistant's reply, such as streaming text, Markdown, and tool calls, is covered by the AI Response Rendering Pattern, and approving the assistant's actions by the AI Action Review Pattern. This guide works with or without them.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has chat, message, or composer components, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend them to meet this guide. Keep their APIs.
  2. Otherwise use plain HTML: a <form> with a labelled <textarea> and one submit button, a list for the transcript, and a <nav> for the conversation list.
  3. Choose what the task needs: the conversation list, attachments, quick actions, and the optional capabilities at the end. Leave out the rest.

Add no dependency, such as a chat UI kit or an autosize library, without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Layout

  • The page is a full-height grid, 100dvh tall with 100vh as the fallback: the conversation list's column, when it's docked, and the chat column.
  • The chat column has three rows: the header, the transcript, and the composer. In the chat column only the transcript scrolls (overflow-y: auto, overscroll-behavior: contain); a docked conversation list scrolls inside its own column.
  • Grid and flex items default to min-height: auto, so give the page grid's columns min-height: 0. Without it, a long conversation list or conversation stretches the page and pushes the composer off screen.
  • The header and the composer stay visible because they're outside the transcript's scrolling area, not because of position: fixed. So they never cover the focused element (WCAG 2.4.11), and the composer stays above mobile browser toolbars.
  • A docked conversation list takes its own column and never covers the chat.
  • The transcript is centered and at most 768 px wide. Sizes in this guide are suggested defaults; the project's design wins.
  • At 320 px wide nothing scrolls sideways, apart from code blocks, which scroll inside themselves.

The composer

  • A labelled <textarea> and one submit button. The label can be visually hidden. If a placeholder shows a prompt such as "Message Acme Assistant", the label uses the same words, so voice control users can say what they see.
  • Text is at least 16 px, so iOS Safari doesn't zoom the page when the field gets focus.
  • It grows with its content up to about 8 lines, then scrolls inside: field-sizing: content where the browser supports it, otherwise set the height from scrollHeight on input.
  • Problems with the draft, such as a message that's too long or a rejected file, show as text under the composer, linked to the textarea with aria-describedby.

Enter

Enter sends and Shift+Enter adds a line. Enter that confirms an input method editor (IME) composition never sends, so people typing Japanese, Chinese, or Korean can confirm characters: check isComposing, and keyCode 229, which is how Safari reports that Enter.

When the primary input is touch ((hover: none) and (pointer: coarse)), assume an on-screen keyboard, which has no Shift+Enter, so Enter adds a line and the button sends. That's a heuristic: a tablet with a keyboard may get the new-line default, and touchscreen laptops usually keep Enter to send. An existing Enter-to-send setting overrides it, and the button always sends.

The snippets in this guide are plain JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version. form, textarea, button, transcript, and jumpButton stand for the composer's and the transcript's elements, and conversation for the app's state.

// Enter sends, and Shift+Enter adds a line. enterSends is the product's Enter-to-send // setting, or undefined to use the touch heuristic. const touchPrimary = matchMedia('(hover: none) and (pointer: coarse)');  textarea.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {   if (event.key !== 'Enter' || event.shiftKey) return;   // Enter that confirms an IME composition; Safari reports it as keyCode 229   if (event.isComposing || event.keyCode === 229) return;   // On-screen keyboards have no Shift+Enter, so there Enter adds a line by default   if (!(enterSends ?? !touchPrimary.matches)) return;   event.preventDefault();   // While a reply streams, Enter keeps the draft: the button is Stop   if (!conversation.replyInProgress) form.requestSubmit(); });

Send and Stop

One button sends, and turns into Stop while a reply streams. Stop stops the reply and keeps its text. The textarea stays editable, so the next message can be drafted, but Enter doesn't send until the reply ends or is stopped.

The button never gets the disabled attribute, which would drop focus to the page when its state changes. With nothing to send, it has aria-disabled="true" and does nothing. Its name follows its state: "Send message" or "Stop response". In Stop mode it has formnovalidate, so a required field or other form validation never blocks Stop. It's at least 24 by 24 px; 40 to 44 px is comfortable.

// One submit button that sends, or stops the reply while one streams. It never gets the // disabled attribute, which would drop focus to the page: with nothing to send it's // aria-disabled, and the submit handler ignores it. Call this when a reply starts and ends. function updateComposerButton() {   const stop = conversation.replyInProgress;   button.dataset.mode = stop ? 'stop' : 'send';   button.setAttribute('aria-label', stop ? 'Stop response' : 'Send message');   button.formNoValidate = stop; // form validation, such as a required field, never blocks Stop   const nothingToSend = !stop && textarea.value.trim() === '';   button.setAttribute('aria-disabled', String(nothingToSend)); }  textarea.addEventListener('input', updateComposerButton);

Sending, and failed sends

When the person sends, the message appears in the transcript as sending, and the draft stays in the composer until the server accepts the message. It leaves only if the composer still holds the sent text, so anything typed meanwhile stays. The button is ignored while a message is being sent, so a double press sends once.

If sending fails, the message shows "Not sent" with a Retry button, the draft is still in the composer, and the status region says "Message not sent". Retry sends the message again with the same id, so the server can drop a copy it already has, as when a dropped connection hid that the first attempt arrived. Sending a changed draft instead replaces the failed message.

// The draft leaves the composer only once the server has accepted the message, so a failed // send loses nothing. showMessage() adds the message to the transcript with a new id; // sendMessage() sends it with that id, which Retry reuses, so the server can drop a copy it // already has. announce() writes to the conversation's status region. form.addEventListener('submit', async (event) => {   event.preventDefault();   if (conversation.replyInProgress) return conversation.stop(); // the button is Stop   const text = textarea.value;   if (!text.trim() || form.dataset.sending === 'true') return;   form.dataset.sending = 'true';   const message = showMessage(text, 'sending');   try {     await sendMessage(message); // resolves once the server has accepted the message     message.setStatus('sent');     if (textarea.value === text) textarea.value = ''; // keep a draft typed meanwhile   } catch {     message.setStatus('failed'); // "Not sent" with Retry; the draft is still in the composer     announce('Message not sent.');   }   form.dataset.sending = 'false';   updateComposerButton(); });

Sending doesn't move focus: after Enter it stays in the textarea, and after a press of the button it stays on the button. Don't focus the composer when the page loads on touch devices, where that opens the on-screen keyboard; focus it when the person starts a new conversation or picks a suggested prompt.

Optional parts of the composer:

  • Attachments: a button that opens the file picker. Attached files show as chips with a remove button named for the file ("Remove report.csv"). Type and size checks in the browser are a convenience; the server checks them again. Show file names as text.
  • Quick actions and suggested prompts: buttons that fill the composer and move focus to it, so the person can edit before sending. Suggested prompts in an empty conversation may send at once when they need no editing.
  • Escape: Escape in the composer can stop a streaming reply, unless the chat sits in a dialog or panel that Escape closes.

The transcript

  • Messages appear oldest first, in a list or a series of articles. The transcript isn't a live region.
  • Each message starts with a visually hidden heading that names the speaker, such as "You said:" or "Acme Assistant said:", one level below the conversation's heading. Screen reader users move between messages with the heading key. Don't put aria-label on a message: it would replace the content.
  • The person's messages sit on the end side (right in left-to-right languages) and the assistant's on the start side. Logical properties, such as margin-inline-start, mirror the layout for right-to-left languages, and dir="auto" on the person's messages shows mixed-direction text correctly.
  • The person's messages are plain text with their line breaks (white-space: pre-wrap). Assistant messages go through the project's renderer. Links in messages are underlined.
  • Long text wraps (overflow-wrap: anywhere). A code block scrolls inside itself; one that scrolls and has nothing focusable gets tabindex="0" and a name.
  • Avatars are optional and decorative (alt=""), since the heading names the speaker. Timestamps are optional, in a <time datetime> element.
  • The person's messages can have Edit, which lets them change the message and send it again (see branching), and Copy. Every icon button has a name and is at least 24 by 24 px.

Waiting for a reply

From the moment the message is accepted until the reply's first content appears, show a waiting indicator, such as three dots. The dots are decorative (aria-hidden="true") and static under reduced motion. Hide the indicator as soon as content appears, or when the reply's streaming cursor appears, if the project follows the AI Response Rendering Pattern.

Announcements

One element with role="status" per conversation, visually hidden and present before anything changes, announces one short sentence at a time:

  • "Acme Assistant is responding", once, when a reply starts
  • "Response complete", "Response stopped", or the failure, when it ends
  • "Message not sent", when a send fails

It never reads the streamed text, or the person's own message. After "Response complete", screen reader users find the reply by its heading.

A modal over the chat, such as the conversation overlay, makes this region inert, which hides it from screen readers. Anything that must be heard while a modal is open goes through a status region inside it.

Following new content

The transcript follows new content only while the reader is at the bottom, within about 48 px. Only scrolling up stops following; content that grows below the view never does. It follows instantly, never with smooth scrolling. While the reader is scrolled up, a Jump to latest button shows. It scrolls to the bottom, follows again, and puts focus in the composer, since it hides itself. Sending a message also scrolls to the bottom and follows again.

// The transcript follows new content only while the reader is at the bottom. let pinned = true; let lastTop = 0;  transcript.addEventListener('scroll', () => {   const nearBottom = transcript.scrollHeight - transcript.scrollTop - transcript.clientHeight < 48;   // Only scrolling up unpins, so content that grows below the view never does   pinned = transcript.scrollTop < lastTop ? nearBottom : pinned || nearBottom;   lastTop = transcript.scrollTop;   jumpButton.hidden = pinned; });  // Call after each update, and with true when the person sends a message function followIfPinned(pin = false) {   if (pin) pinned = true;   if (pinned) transcript.scrollTop = transcript.scrollHeight; // instant, never smooth }  jumpButton.addEventListener('click', () => {   textarea.focus(); // the button is about to hide, so focus goes to the composer   followIfPinned(true); });

A conversation opens at its latest message, and loading older messages at the top keeps what's on screen where it is.

The conversation list

The list is navigation: a <nav> labelled "Conversations", with a link for each conversation, since each has its own URL. The open one has aria-current="page". A New chat button at the top starts a conversation and puts focus in the composer.

  • From 1024 px wide, the list is docked: its own grid column, open by default. A toggle in the header opens and closes it, with aria-expanded and aria-controls. When closed, the column is hidden (the hidden attribute or display: none), not only moved off screen.
  • Below 1024 px, it opens as a modal: native <dialog> opened with showModal(), or the Dialog guide's model. It has a visible Close button, closes on Escape, on a backdrop click, and when a conversation is chosen, and returns focus to the toggle.
  • The list scrolls inside its column while docked (overflow-y: auto), and inside the dialog below 1024 px, so a long list never stretches the page.
  • If the docked list comes before the chat in the page, the page starts with a skip link to the chat (WCAG 2.4.1).
  • When the window crosses 1024 px, react to a matchMedia change, not to resize events. If the overlay is open when the window gets wider, close it and move focus to the same item in the docked list.
  • In a single-page app, opening a conversation moves focus to its heading (tabindex="-1") and updates document.title. A reply that's still running keeps going on the server, and shows when the person returns, never in the conversation they switched to. Drafts are kept per conversation.

Optional: groups such as Today and Previous 7 days, under headings; rename, pin, and delete in a More actions menu per item, with delete asking first or offering undo; and a filter field whose number of matches is announced politely.

The header

  • The conversation's title, as the page's main heading or a visually hidden heading such as "Chat", and in document.title.
  • The list toggle, New chat, and other actions, such as an assistant or model picker and a More actions menu. Clearing a conversation asks first or offers undo.
  • On phones: the toggle, the title, and New chat; the rest goes in the More actions menu.

Saved state

  • Messages and conversations live on the server, not in the browser's storage, and the open conversation is in the URL.
  • Whether the docked list is open can be saved under the app's own storage prefix, for example acme.chat.sidebar, where acme stands for that prefix. Apply it before the first paint, with a cookie the server reads or a small inline script, so the layout doesn't jump.
  • Drafts can be saved per conversation, in sessionStorage or where the app keeps drafts, and cleared once the message is sent.
  • With server rendering, render the conversation on the server, so it shows before scripts run.

Phones

  • Pad the header's top and the composer's bottom with env(safe-area-inset-top) and env(safe-area-inset-bottom), and add viewport-fit=cover to the viewport meta tag.
  • Add interactive-widget=resizes-content to the same tag, so browsers that support it, such as Chrome on Android, shrink the layout when the on-screen keyboard opens and the composer stays above it. iOS Safari keeps the layout size and scrolls the focused field into view.
  • Targets are at least 24 by 24 px; 44 px is comfortable for touch.

Motion

Motion is optional. New messages fade in over 200 ms with cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1), only when they arrive while the page is open, never for the history on load. The docked list slides in over 250 ms. Following new content never animates. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, nothing slides or fades, and the waiting dots are static.

Colors

Suggested defaults for projects without a design. The project's tokens win; check its colors meet the same contrast, including in dark mode.

  • The person's messages: white text on #2563eb (5.2:1), or on #1d4ed8 in dark mode (6.7:1). Links in them are underlined in the text color.
  • The assistant's text: #111827 on white (17.7:1), or #f3f4f6 on #111827 in dark mode (16.1:1). Assistant messages can do without a bubble.
  • Muted text, such as timestamps, statuses, and the placeholder: #6b7280 (4.8:1), or #9ca3af in dark mode (7.0:1).
  • Links: #1d4ed8 (6.7:1), or #93c5fd in dark mode (9.8:1), always underlined.
  • The composer's edge: #6b7280 (4.8:1, and 3.7:1 on the dark page). Focus indicators: #2563eb, or #60a5fa in dark mode.
  • Errors: #b91c1c (6.5:1), or #fca5a5 in dark mode (9.4:1).

Bubble tails and shadows are optional decoration; the side and the speaker heading tell messages apart.

Optional capabilities

Add these only when the product needs them.

  • Branching helps when people edit an earlier question and expect the original answer kept. Editing creates a new version of the message, which shows "2 of 3" with Previous and Next version buttons; the transcript below follows the chosen version. Announce the change.
  • Pinning helps when people return to a few conversations often. Pinned conversations sit in their own group at the top of the list.
  • History search helps when people ask where an earlier conversation went. A search over all conversations, with results that link to the conversation and its matching message. Announce the number of results.
  • Keyboard shortcuts help people who chat all day, for example a shortcut for New chat and one to the composer. Avoid keys the browser and screen readers use, list the shortcuts in the interface, and let people turn off single-key shortcuts (WCAG 2.1.4).
  • Embedded chat: a launcher button opens the chat in a modal dialog (see the Dialog guide) or a side panel. A panel moves focus in when it opens, closes with Escape, returns focus to the launcher, and leaves the page usable.

Working with the other AI guides

  • With the AI Response Rendering Pattern, this layout owns the shell, the Send and Stop button, Edit on the person's messages, following new content, and the conversation's status region. The pattern owns the inside of each assistant message, including Copy, Regenerate, and feedback, and announces through this layout's status region.
  • With the AI Action Review Pattern, this layout places the review: a card in the transcript for low-risk actions, or a side panel, drawer, or dialog for the rest.

Edge cases

  • A reply that doesn't start: give the request a time limit, for example 30 seconds, and show the failure with Retry when it runs out. Tell a timeout from other failures by the signal's reason, as the Dialog guide does.
  • Offline: a send while offline fails like any other, with Not sent and Retry. Optionally, retry once the browser is back online, and say so.
  • Long drafts: if the product limits message length, show the count near the limit and explain an over-limit draft under the composer. Never cut the draft.
  • Reloads: after a reload during a reply, show what the server saved, and continue the stream if the backend supports it.
  • Long conversations: virtualize the transcript only when conversations get long (several hundred messages), and keep the newest messages and any focused element rendered.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Enter sends and Shift+Enter adds a line; Enter that confirms an IME composition (Japanese, Chinese, Korean) doesn't send, including in Safari
  • [ ] With a phone's on-screen keyboard, Enter adds a line and the button sends; an Enter-to-send setting overrides that on every device
  • [ ] While a reply streams, the button is Stop and keeps focus, form validation never blocks it, Stop keeps the reply's text, and Enter in the composer keeps the draft without sending
  • [ ] With nothing to send, the button is aria-disabled, stays focusable, and does nothing
  • [ ] A message that fails to send shows Not sent with Retry, the draft is still in the composer, and a screen reader hears that it wasn't sent
  • [ ] A draft typed while a message is being sent stays in the composer, and a double press sends once
  • [ ] The transcript follows new content only at the bottom; scrolled up, it stays put, and Jump to latest scrolls down and puts focus in the composer
  • [ ] A screen reader can move between messages by heading, hears that a reply started and ended, and never hears the streamed text
  • [ ] The header and the composer never cover the focused element, and on phones the composer stays above the browser's toolbars and the on-screen keyboard
  • [ ] With a long conversation list and a long conversation, each scrolls on its own, and the composer stays on screen
  • [ ] Below 1024 px the conversation list opens as a modal with a Close button, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the toggle; a closed list can't be reached with Tab
  • [ ] The open conversation has aria-current and is named in the page title, and a skip link moves past a long conversation list
  • [ ] At 320 px wide and at 400% zoom nothing scrolls sideways, and right-to-left languages mirror the layout
  • [ ] With reduced motion, nothing slides or fades, and following new content never animates
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens, and text, the composer's edge, and focus indicators meet the contrast minimums

See also

  • AI Response Rendering Pattern: what goes inside an assistant message.
  • AI Action Review Pattern: approving the actions the assistant proposes.
  • Modal Dialog: for the conversation overlay and for confirmations.
  • Sidebar Navigation: when the conversation list sits next to the app's own navigation.
  • Command Palette: quick prompts, commands, and switching conversations from the keyboard.
  • Text Input: label, hint, and error conventions for the composer.
  • Toast Notifications: feedback outside the conversation, such as a deleted conversation with Undo.
  • Select and Combobox: an assistant or model picker.
  • Navigation Bar: when the chat sits under the site's own header.
  • Button: the composer's button and the header's actions.

These are suggestions; the layout works with any components you choose.
excerpt: A chat layout for an AI assistant: a conversation list, a transcript that stays put while you read, and a composer whose Send button turns into Stop. A message that fails to send stays in the input with a retry.

title: Pricing Table
body:
A pricing section answers three questions: what each plan costs, what it includes, and which one to pick. Its common mistakes are about trust: savings badges that don't match the prices, a toggle read as "switch, on", prices read as "slash mo", and three cards squeezed side by side on a tablet. This guide covers the plans, the billing choice, the prices, and the calls to action, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has pricing cards or a plan picker, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend them to meet this guide. Keep their APIs.
  2. Take plans and prices from its billing system; never compute a price it doesn't charge.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Plans

  • Plans and prices come from the project's billing system (Stripe, Paddle, the app's own), with each price in the currency's smallest unit, such as cents. Prices are rendered on the server.
  • Each plan is an <article> named by its heading (<h3> under the section's <h2>), with its price, a sentence on who it's for, one call to action, and what it includes.
  • A "Most popular" badge is plain text, not a live region, and only on a plan that is the most popular. On phones, a plan shown first is first in the page too, not moved with CSS order, so the reading and focus order match what's shown.

The billing choice

  • Two options, Monthly and Yearly, are one choice: a radio group (<fieldset> with the <legend> "Billing"), drawn as a segmented control. The radios stay real: the group is one Tab stop, the arrows choose, and screen readers say something like "Yearly, radio button, 2 of 2". A switch would be read as "on" or "off" and can only name one side.
  • Monthly is chosen by default, or whichever period the server renders. The Yearly option's label says the best saving ("Save up to 19%"), or the one saving when every plan saves the same ("Save 17%").
  • Without script the choice can't change the prices, so the server renders one period's prices and the script shows the choice.
  • After Back, the browser restores the checked option without an input or change event, and Chromium does it only after the page's scripts and DOMContentLoaded have run (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). Work the prices out from the checked option when the script runs and again on pageshow.
  • The focused option shows a focus ring on :focus: WebKit doesn't match :focus-visible on a radio the arrows moved to (checked). In forced colors, which replace backgrounds, the chosen option takes the system's Highlight.
  • Choosing needs no announcement: the radio says its new state, and the prices change where people read them next.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<!-- Prices are in cents. The server renders monthly prices and links; the script shows the choice. --> <fieldset class="billing" hidden>   <legend>Billing</legend>   <div class="billing-options">     <label><input type="radio" name="billing" value="monthly" checked> Monthly</label>     <label><input type="radio" name="billing" value="yearly"> Yearly <span class="billing-saving"></span></label>   </div> </fieldset> <div class="plans">   <article class="plan" aria-labelledby="plan-starter" data-monthly="900" data-yearly="8900">     <h3 id="plan-starter">Starter</h3>     <p><span class="plan-amount">$9</span> <span class="plan-period">per month</span></p>     <p class="plan-saving"></p>     <a href="/signup?plan=starter&billing=monthly">Get started<span class="visually-hidden"> with Starter</span></a>   </article>   <article class="plan" aria-labelledby="plan-pro" data-monthly="2900" data-yearly="27900">     <p class="plan-badge">Most popular</p>     <h3 id="plan-pro">Professional</h3>     <p><span class="plan-amount">$29</span> <span class="plan-period">per month</span></p>     <p class="plan-saving"></p>     <a href="/signup?plan=pro&billing=monthly">Get started<span class="visually-hidden"> with Professional</span></a>   </article>   <!-- more plans the same way; one without data-monthly (Contact sales) is left alone --> </div> 
/* The billing choice is a radio group drawn as a segmented control: the radios stay real, so    the arrows move between them, and each label shows the state. */ .billing {   border: 0;   margin: 0;   padding: 0; } .billing-options {   border: 1px solid var(--control-border); /* 3:1 against the page */   border-radius: 999px;   display: inline-flex;   padding: 4px; } .billing-options label {   border-radius: 999px;   cursor: pointer;   padding: 8px 16px;   position: relative; } .billing-options input {   inset: 0;   margin: 0;   opacity: 0;   position: absolute; } .billing-options label:has(input:checked) {   background: var(--selected-background);   color: var(--selected-text); } /* :focus, not :focus-visible: WebKit doesn't match :focus-visible on a radio the arrows moved to */ .billing-options label:has(input:focus) {   outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring);   outline-offset: 2px; } /* Forced colors replace backgrounds, so the chosen option takes the system's highlight */ @media (forced-colors: active) {   .billing-options label:has(input:checked) {     background: Highlight;     color: HighlightText;     forced-color-adjust: none;   } } /* Cards wrap to two and one columns on their own, never narrower than 16rem */ .plans {   display: grid;   gap: 24px;   grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(16rem, 100%), 1fr)); } 
// Prices and savings come from each plan's prices, so "Save 19%" can't drift from them. Amounts // are whole cents, which keeps the percentages exact, and savings round down, so they never // claim more than a plan saves. A free plan has nothing to save, so it's left out of them. const billing = document.querySelector('.billing'); const plans = [...document.querySelectorAll('.plan[data-monthly]')]; const money = new Intl.NumberFormat(document.documentElement.lang || undefined, { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD', trailingZeroDisplay: 'stripIfInteger' }); const perUnit = 10 ** money.resolvedOptions().maximumFractionDigits; const saving = (plan) => Math.floor(((plan.dataset.monthly * 12 - plan.dataset.yearly) * 100) / (plan.dataset.monthly * 12));  function render() {   const period = billing.querySelector('input:checked')?.value === 'yearly' ? 'yearly' : 'monthly';   for (const plan of plans) {     plan.querySelector('.plan-amount').textContent = money.format(plan.dataset[period] / perUnit);     plan.querySelector('.plan-period').textContent = period === 'yearly' ? 'per year' : 'per month';     plan.querySelector('.plan-saving').textContent = period === 'yearly' && saving(plan) > 0 ? `Save ${saving(plan)}% compared with monthly` : '';     // The call to action takes the chosen period to signup     const link = plan.querySelector('a[href]');     const query = new URLSearchParams(link.search);     query.set('billing', period);     link.search = query;   }   const savings = plans.filter((plan) => plan.dataset.monthly > 0).map(saving);   const best = Math.max(0, ...savings);   billing.querySelector('.billing-saving').textContent = best === 0 ? '' : savings.every((s) => s === best) ? `Save ${best}%` : `Save up to ${best}%`; } billing.hidden = false; billing.addEventListener('change', render); // After Back, the browser restores the checked option without a change event, and Chromium // does it only after this script has run addEventListener('pageshow', render); render();

Prices and savings

  • Prices are formatted with Intl.NumberFormat for the currency and the page's language; trailingZeroDisplay: "stripIfInteger" shows "$29" and "$9.99" (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit).
  • The period is written out, "per month" or "per year"; abbreviations are read letter by letter or as "slash mo". Say whether tax is included where that's required.
  • Savings are claims, so they come from the prices: (12 × monthly − yearly) ÷ (12 × monthly), worked out in the smallest unit, so a plan that saves exactly 20% says 20 (in floating point it comes out at 19.999…%), and rounded down, so they never claim more than a plan saves. The example plans save 17.6%, 19.8%, and 16.7%: "Save 17%", "Save 19%", and "Save 16%". Don't store a separate discount figure that can drift from the prices.
  • A plan without a fixed price ("Contact sales") is left out of the calculation, and so is a free plan, which has nothing to save: dividing by its monthly price of 0 made the label "Save up to NaN%" (checked).

Calls to action

  • Calls to action go to signup or checkout pages, so they're links, with no loading or disabled state of their own. The highlighted plan's is the primary one.
  • They take the chosen period to signup: the script sets billing=yearly or billing=monthly on each plan's link (or the billing system's price id for that period), and the server renders the default period's links. Otherwise signup can't tell which price was chosen.
  • Their visible text comes first in their name: "Get started", with "with Professional" visually hidden after it, so voice control users can say what they see (WCAG 2.5.3) and screen readers can tell them apart.
  • "Start free trial" only on a plan with a trial; otherwise "Get started" or "Contact sales".

Features

  • Each plan's features are a list. A feature it doesn't include says so in text, such as a visually hidden "Not included:" before it, or the list holds only what's included, starting with "Everything in Starter, plus:".
  • Check and cross icons are aria-hidden="true" and meet 3:1: a #047857 check is 5.5:1 on white and a #6b7280 cross 4.8:1, where #10b981 and #9ca3af are 2.5:1.

Layout

  • The cards wrap on their own with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(16rem, 100%), 1fr)): three or four side by side on wide screens, two on a tablet, one on a phone, without a breakpoint. Three fixed columns at 768 px would leave cards about 230 px wide.
  • Rows that line up across cards (the price, the call to action, the features) can use grid-template-rows: subgrid; it's optional.
  • A full comparison is a real <table> with a column per plan and a row header per feature, as in the Data Table guide.

Motion

  • Motion is optional: prices can fade over 150 ms when they change, and cards can lift on hover. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, nothing moves; prices change at once.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • Cards with 24 to 40 px of padding and a 12 to 16 px radius; the plan's name 20 to 28 px; the price 40 to 56 px.
  • Colors: #111827 text (17.7:1 on white), #4b5563 muted text (7.6:1); a primary call to action in #2563eb with white text (5.2:1), since #3b82f6 is only 3.7:1; the segmented control's edge #6b7280 (4.8:1), the chosen option #111827 with white text, and a #2563eb focus ring. Check the project's own colors the same way.

Edge cases

  • A plan without a fixed price ("Contact sales") is left out of the prices and the savings
  • A free plan (0 and 0) has nothing to save and is left out of the savings
  • Prices with cents keep them ("$9.99"); whole prices drop ".00"
  • Every plan saves the same: the Yearly label says "Save 17%", not "up to"
  • Two or four plans: the grid wraps on its own
  • A currency without cents (JPY): the smallest unit is the whole yen, which the formatter's fraction digits give
  • No yearly prices at all: leave the billing choice out
  • A promotion that ends: say its end date in text, with no countdown that pressures

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Each plan is an article named by its heading, with its price, what it includes, and one call to action
  • [ ] The billing choice is a fieldset with a legend and two radios, drawn as a segmented control: one Tab stop, the arrows choose, and the focused option shows a focus ring in every browser
  • [ ] Without script, the page shows one period's prices and no choice
  • [ ] Choosing Yearly updates every plan's price and period at once; a plan without a fixed price is left alone
  • [ ] Prices are formatted for the currency and the locale, and periods are written out ("per month"), not abbreviated
  • [ ] Savings are worked out from the prices in the currency's smallest unit and rounded down, leaving out free plans; the Yearly label says "Save up to" the best one, or "Save" when all are equal
  • [ ] After Back, the prices and the links match the restored choice
  • [ ] Calls to action are links whose names start with their visible text, with the plan's name added out of sight, and they take the chosen period to signup
  • [ ] Included and not included features say so in text, and their icons are hidden from screen readers and meet 3:1
  • [ ] A "Most popular" badge is plain text, is true, and is not a live region
  • [ ] Cards wrap to fewer columns on their own, a plan shown first on phones comes first in the page, and nothing scrolls sideways at 320 px wide
  • [ ] In forced colors, the chosen billing option is still visible
  • [ ] Text meets 4.5:1, and the segmented control's edge and focus ring 3:1
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Button: the calls to action's styles and states.
  • Landing Page Layout (Marketing): the marketing page a pricing section usually sits in.
  • Data Table (Sortable, Paginated, Filterable): a full comparison as a table.

These are suggestions; the pricing table works on its own.
excerpt: Pricing plans with a monthly or yearly billing choice: a radio group drawn as a segmented control, prices and savings worked out from each plan's prices, and calls to action that are links.

title: Login & Registration Forms with Validation
body:
Sign-in and registration are where accessibility, security, and privacy meet. This guide covers the sign-in and registration forms, the password reset request, and their messages. It follows NIST SP 800-63B-4 for passwords, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project uses an authentication service, its own backend or a provider or library such as Auth0, Clerk, Supabase Auth, Firebase Auth, Amazon Cognito, or Auth.js, follow its password rules, rate limits, and passkey support, and use its components or SDK. This guide fills the gaps; it doesn't override the service's rules.
  2. Map the service's error codes to this guide's public messages. Never show messages that reveal whether an account exists, such as "user not found" or "email already in use". If the service can't avoid revealing it, tell the user about the conflict instead of shipping it.
  3. Build on the project's form, field, and button components, and its validation (the Form Validation Pattern).

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

The forms

  • Sign in: email (type="email", autocomplete="username"), password (autocomplete="current-password"), Show password, an optional Remember me, Sign in, a "Forgot your password?" link, and optional passkey and social sign-in. The password is checked for presence only: no length or character rules at sign-in, so accounts made under older rules still work.
  • Registration: one full name field (autocomplete="name"), required but with no minimum length, since some names are one character; email (autocomplete="username"); a new password (autocomplete="new-password") with the requirements indicator; an optional confirmation; terms, if the product needs them; and Create account.
  • Password reset request: email, and the same confirmation for every request.
  • Each form is a <form method="post"> named by its heading (aria-labelledby), with a status region at the top. Posting matters: a form sent before its script runs, on a slow connection or a server-rendered page before hydration, would otherwise use GET and put the email and password in the URL, where history and server logs keep them.
  • The page title says which form it is, such as "Sign in, Acme". Switching between sign-in and registration moves focus to the new form's heading.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<!-- method="post": a form sent before its script runs never puts the password in the URL --> <form id="sign-in" method="post" action="/sign-in" aria-labelledby="sign-in-title">   <h1 id="sign-in-title">Sign in</h1>   <p class="form-status" role="status"></p>   <label for="sign-in-email">Email address</label>   <input id="sign-in-email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="username" required>   <label for="sign-in-password">Password</label>   <div class="password-field">     <input id="sign-in-password" name="password" type="password" autocomplete="current-password"       spellcheck="false" autocapitalize="none" required>     <button type="button" class="password-toggle" aria-pressed="false"       aria-controls="sign-in-password">Show password</button>   </div>   <button type="submit">Sign in</button>   <p><a href="/forgot-password">Forgot your password?</a></p> </form>

Passwords

  • The minimum length comes from the auth service. Otherwise, NIST SP 800-63B-4: at least 15 characters when the password is the only sign-in factor, and at least 8 when a second factor is always required. Count Unicode code points.
  • Accept at least 64 characters, spaces, all printable characters, and Unicode, and don't trim or truncate them.
  • No composition rules: never ask for digits, symbols, or mixed case.
  • Reject common and breached passwords; the full check runs on the server.
  • At registration and reset, a requirements indicator says whether the password is too short, too common, or meets the requirements. It never says "strong" from length: "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" is long, but easy to guess. A pattern-aware strength estimator the project already has may rate instead. Screen readers hear the status when it changes, through the form's status region, not on every keystroke.
// The requirements indicator's state. MIN_LENGTH comes from the auth service, or the // NIST SP 800-63B-4 default for password-only sign-in. isCommonPassword() checks a short // list on the client; the full breached-password check runs on the server. const MIN_LENGTH = 15;  function getPasswordRequirementState(password, isCommonPassword) {   const length = [...password].length; // count Unicode code points, not UTF-16 units   if (length === 0) return 'none';   if (length < MIN_LENGTH) return 'too-short';   if (isCommonPassword(password)) return 'too-common';   return 'meets-requirements'; }

Show password

  • A <button type="button"> next to the field, named "Show password", with aria-pressed. Its name stays the same, screen readers announce its state, and focus stays on it. A "Show password" checkbox works too.
  • Password fields have spellcheck="false" and autocapitalize="none". Shown as text, a password could otherwise reach a browser's online spell-check service (Chrome's Enhanced Spell Check and Microsoft Editor, when turned on; reported in 2022).
  • The password is hidden again when the form is sent or reset, and when the page comes back from the back/forward cache, so it's never left showing.
// The show-password button: a toggle with a name that stays the same and aria-pressed, so // screen readers announce its state, and focus stays on it. The password is hidden again // when the form is sent or reset, and when the page comes back from the back/forward cache. const password = document.getElementById('sign-in-password'); const toggle = document.querySelector('[aria-controls="sign-in-password"]');  function setShown(shown) {   password.type = shown ? 'text' : 'password';   toggle.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(shown)); }  toggle.addEventListener('click', () => setShown(password.type === 'password')); password.form.addEventListener('submit', () => setShown(false)); password.form.addEventListener('reset', () => setShown(false)); // hiding is always safe window.addEventListener('pageshow', (event) => {   if (event.persisted) setShown(false); });

Messages that stay generic

These never reveal whether an email has an account, and read the same for every account:

  • Rejected sign-in: "Email or password is incorrect", without saying which field was wrong.
  • Network or service failure: "Unable to sign in right now. Try again shortly". It doesn't blame the password, so an outage never sends people to reset it.
  • After registration: "Check your email to continue", for new and existing emails alike; the backend emails the existing account's owner instead. This needs email verification: if the product signs new users in immediately, registration can't hide whether an email exists, so raise that tradeoff.
  • Password reset request: "If an account exists for this email, we've sent a reset link".
  • Rate limit: "Too many attempts. Wait a few minutes and try again".

Sign-in results show at the top of the form, in its status region, with the email kept. Field errors stay specific: "Enter your email address", "Use at least 15 characters", "This password is too common. Choose a different one", "This password has appeared in a data breach. Choose a different one", and "Passwords must match".

Sending

  • Validation runs first, with the Form Validation Pattern's timing.
  • While the request runs, the button has aria-disabled="true", ignores another press, and keeps focus, and the status region says "Signing in…". Don't disable the fields or the button: disabling the focused element drops focus to the page in Chromium and Firefox (checked).
  • The request has a time limit, 30 seconds suggested. A timeout or a dropped connection gets the network message, never the wrong-details one.
  • On success, go on to the app, or to the "Check your email" step. On failure, keep the email, show the message, and make the button work again.
// Sending the sign-in. The button keeps focus (aria-disabled, not disabled), a second submit // while one runs is ignored, and the status region says what's happening. Wrong details and // a failed connection get different messages, and neither says which field was wrong. // signIn() stands for the app's request and onSignedIn() for its next step; map the auth // service's answers to these messages. const form = document.getElementById('sign-in'); const button = form.querySelector('[type="submit"]'); const status = form.querySelector('[role="status"]'); const messages = {   401: 'Email or password is incorrect',   429: 'Too many attempts. Wait a few minutes and try again', };  form.addEventListener('submit', async (event) => {   event.preventDefault();   if (button.getAttribute('aria-disabled') === 'true') return;   button.setAttribute('aria-disabled', 'true');   status.textContent = 'Signing in…';   try {     const response = await signIn(new FormData(form), { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) });     if (response.ok) return onSignedIn(response);     status.textContent = messages[response.status] ?? 'Unable to sign in right now. Try again shortly';   } catch {     status.textContent = 'Unable to sign in right now. Try again shortly';   } finally {     button.removeAttribute('aria-disabled');   } });

Password managers, paste, and passkeys

  • autocomplete="username" on the email that identifies the account, also when it holds an email address; current-password at sign-in; new-password at registration and reset; and one-time-code on verification codes.
  • Never block paste or autofill (WCAG 2.2 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication).
  • Passkeys (optional): a "Sign in with a passkey" button, and passkey autofill with autocomplete="username webauthn" on the email field. If the prompt is cancelled or fails, focus returns to the passkey button, a short generic message shows, and the password form stays.

Accessibility

  • Labels are visible, and required and optional fields say so in words.
  • Field errors follow the Form Validation Pattern: text next to the field, aria-describedby and aria-invalid, and no live regions. A failed submit moves focus to the first invalid field.
  • One status region per form, for "Signing in…", the sign-in results, and the requirement status.
  • Buttons, Show password included, are at least 24 by 24 px (44 px suggested on touch), and text is at least 16 px on phones.

Layout and motion

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • A card at most 420 px wide, centered, with 48 px padding from 768 px wide and 24 px below.
  • On phones, the card fills the width minus 16 px gutters. Fields and buttons are 48 px tall.
  • Motion is optional: a 200 ms fade when switching forms. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, changes are instant.

Edge cases

  • An email that already has an account: registration shows the same next step as for a new email, and the backend emails the account's owner a sign-in or reset link instead.
  • An older account whose password is shorter than today's minimum still signs in; ask for a new password after sign-in only if the auth service requires it.
  • A password filled by a password manager or pasted is accepted.
  • Spaces and Unicode in a password are kept as typed, never trimmed.
  • Too many attempts: the generic rate-limit message, worded the same whether or not the account exists.
  • A passkey prompt cancelled or failed: the password form stays, and focus returns to the passkey button.
  • A request that never answers ends at the time limit with the network message, and pressing Sign in again retries.
  • A product that signs new users in immediately can't hide at registration whether an email has an account: raise that tradeoff with the user.
  • Long emails and names scroll inside their fields, and nothing is cut off.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Each form posts (method="post"), so a form sent before its script runs never puts a password in the URL
  • [ ] Sign-in accepts any non-empty password; registration and reset apply the length, common-password, and breach rules, with no composition rules
  • [ ] Passwords of 64 or more characters, spaces, and Unicode are accepted as typed
  • [ ] The requirements indicator never says "strong" from length alone, and screen readers hear its status when it changes
  • [ ] A failed sign-in says "Email or password is incorrect", a network or service failure says "Unable to sign in right now", and the email stays filled in
  • [ ] Registration, password reset, and rate-limit messages read the same whether or not the account exists
  • [ ] Password managers can save and fill the credentials, and paste works in every field
  • [ ] Show password keeps its name and focus, shows its state with aria-pressed, and the password is hidden again when the form is sent or reset, or the page comes back
  • [ ] Password fields have spellcheck="false"
  • [ ] While signing in, the button keeps focus with aria-disabled, a second press sends nothing, and the status region says "Signing in…"
  • [ ] Field errors follow the Form Validation Pattern, and a failed submit moves focus to the first invalid field
  • [ ] Passkey sign-in, if offered, falls back to the password form when it's cancelled or fails
  • [ ] The forms work at 320 px wide, with 16 px text on phones
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Text Input Field: the email and password fields.
  • Select and Combobox: a country or a language in registration forms.
  • Button: Sign in, Show password, and link-style actions.
  • Form Validation Pattern: when field errors appear, and where focus goes when a form is submitted.

These are suggestions; the forms work with any components and auth service.
excerpt: Sign-in and registration forms that follow current NIST password guidance, never reveal whether an email has an account, work with password managers and passkeys, and keep passwords out of URLs, spell-check services, and plain view.

title: Toast Notifications
body:
Toasts tell people what just happened without interrupting them. Their usual failures can't be seen: messages screen readers never hear, an Undo that's gone before a keyboard user reaches it, a stack that covers what has focus, and an Escape that closes the wrong thing. This guide covers when to use a toast, the stack and its live regions, timing, keys, and focus, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a toast or notification component, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API.
  2. Otherwise build one stack for the app, with a small API such as showToast({ title, description, variant, action }).

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

When to use a toast

  • A toast is brief news about something that just happened, often with one action: "Message sent", "File deleted" with Undo, "Link copied".
  • Errors people must fix show next to what they concern, as in the Form Validation guide; anything people must read or decide before going on is a dialog.
  • Repeats are grouped ("3 files deleted"), and the same message within a second or so shows once.

The stack and its live regions

  • One <section> named "Notifications" holds the toasts, newest last, at the bottom of the screen: at the inline end on wide screens, and as wide as the screen less 32 px on phones. A top corner would sit over the header's own controls (an account menu, a theme choice) and could hide one entirely when it has focus (2.4.11), so toasts go to the bottom on every screen. On a page with a fixed bottom bar, such as a purchase bar or a tab bar, the script measures the bar and sets --bottom-bar-height to its height, and the stack sits above it, so the bar's controls stay visible.
  • Two live regions read the toasts out: role="status" (polite), and role="alert" for errors that need attention now; warnings and the rest are polite. Both are in the page, empty, from the start, outside the section, and never hidden: a live region inside a hidden element drops out of the accessibility tree (checked in Chromium). Neither is atomic (aria-atomic="false"): both roles are atomic unless told otherwise, and an atomic region is read out whole each time a message is added, the earlier ones still in it included. Each toast's words go into one of them, and go when the toast goes; the toasts themselves aren't in a live region, so nothing is nested.
  • At most three toasts show at once, one on phones. The rest wait, and show in order when there's room, read out as they show. When the screen narrows, the toasts already showing stay and new ones wait; when it widens, waiting toasts fill the free places in order.
  • Layers: toasts sit above sticky bars and dropdowns and below modals, in the project's layer scale. While a modal is open, the page behind it is inert, toasts and their live regions included, so the result of the modal's task shows in the modal (the Modal Dialog guide's status message) or after it closes.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<!-- At the end of <body>. The section shows the toasts; the two live regions read them out.      Both regions are in the page, empty, from the start and are never hidden: one polite, one      for errors that need attention now. Neither is atomic, so a new message is read out alone. --> <section class="toasts" aria-label="Notifications" aria-keyshortcuts="F8" hidden>   <ol></ol> </section> <div class="visually-hidden" role="status" aria-atomic="false" id="toast-status"></div> <div class="visually-hidden" role="alert" aria-atomic="false" id="toast-alert"></div> 
/* At the bottom of every screen, so toasts never cover the header's controls, and above a fixed    bottom bar, whose height the script measures. The project's layer for toasts puts them above    sticky bars and dropdowns, and below modals. */ .toasts {   inline-size: min(380px, calc(100% - 32px));   inset-block-end: calc(16px + var(--bottom-bar-height, 0px));   inset-inline-end: 16px;   position: fixed;   z-index: var(--layer-toasts); } .toasts ol {   display: grid;   gap: 12px;   list-style: none;   margin: 0;   padding: 0; } .toast {   align-items: center;   background: var(--toast-surface);   border: 1px solid var(--toast-border);   border-radius: 10px;   display: flex;   flex-wrap: wrap;   gap: 8px;   padding: 12px 16px; } .toast p {   flex: 1 1 12rem;   margin: 0; } /* Only F8 focuses a toast, so the ring shows on :focus */ .toast:focus {   outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring);   outline-offset: 2px; } .toast button {   min-block-size: 32px;   min-inline-size: 32px; } /* On whatever scrolls the page (here :root; in an app shell, its scroll container): the end of    the content has room for a fixed bottom bar and the stack, and a focused element scrolls clear    of both. Where the project already keeps room for its bar, count it once. The script keeps both    heights up to date. */ :root {   padding-block-end: calc(var(--bottom-bar-height, 0px) + var(--toast-stack-height, 0px));   scroll-padding-block-end: calc(var(--bottom-bar-height, 0px) + var(--toast-stack-height, 0px)); } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {   .toast {     animation: toast-in 250ms cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);   } } @keyframes toast-in {   from {     opacity: 0;     translate: 0 8px;   } } 
// showToast({ title, description, variant, action: { label, onSelect }, duration }). Errors and // toasts with an action stay until they're dismissed; the others leave after `duration` (see the // timers). At most three show, one on phones; the rest wait in order, and are read out when they // show. Toasts already showing stay when the screen narrows. const region = document.querySelector('.toasts'); const list = region.querySelector('ol'); const politeRegion = document.getElementById('toast-status'); const alertRegion = document.getElementById('toast-alert'); const fallbackFocus = document.querySelector('main'); // tabindex="-1", as the skip link's target const timers = new Map(); // toast → { remaining, started, id } const messages = new Map(); // toast → its text in a live region const waiting = []; const wide = matchMedia('(min-width: 48rem)'); let returnTo = null; // where focus was before it entered the stack  function showToast(toast) {   waiting.push(toast);   fill(); }  // Shows waiting toasts, in order, while there's room function fill() {   while (waiting.length && list.children.length < (wide.matches ? 3 : 1)) add(waiting.shift()); } wide.addEventListener('change', fill);  function add(toast) {   const item = Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { className: `toast toast-${toast.variant ?? 'info'}`, tabIndex: -1 });   const text = Object.assign(document.createElement('p'), { textContent: [toast.title, toast.description].filter(Boolean).join(' ') });   item.append(text);   if (toast.action) item.append(button(toast.action.label, () => { toast.action.onSelect(); dismiss(item); }));   item.append(button('Dismiss', () => dismiss(item)));   list.append(item);   region.hidden = false;   // Errors go to the alert region, the rest to the polite one; an action says how to reach it   const message = Object.assign(document.createElement('p'), { textContent: toast.action ? `${text.textContent} Press F8 for ${toast.action.label}.` : text.textContent });   (toast.variant === 'error' ? alertRegion : politeRegion).append(message);   messages.set(item, message);   if (toast.action || toast.variant === 'error') return;   timers.set(item, { remaining: toast.duration ?? 5000, id: null });   update(); }  function button(label, onClick) {   const element = Object.assign(document.createElement('button'), { type: 'button', textContent: label });   element.addEventListener('click', onClick);   return element; }  // Focus goes back to where it came from, or to the main content when that can't take it (it was // removed, disabled, hidden, or made inert) function restoreFocus() {   returnTo?.focus();   if (document.activeElement !== returnTo) fallbackFocus?.focus(); }  function dismiss(item) {   // Focus goes to the newest other toast, or back to where it came from   if (item.contains(document.activeElement)) {     const next = [...list.children].filter((other) => other !== item).at(-1);     if (next) next.focus();     else restoreFocus();   }   clearTimeout(timers.get(item)?.id);   timers.delete(item);   messages.get(item).remove();   messages.delete(item);   item.remove();   region.hidden = list.children.length === 0;   fill();   update(); }

Timing

  • Errors and toasts with an action stay until they're dismissed: an Undo that disappears before a keyboard or screen reader user reaches it fails 2.2.1. The others leave after about 5 seconds (4 to 6 suggested, longer for longer text).
  • The timers pause while the pointer is over the stack, while focus is in it, and while the page is hidden, and go on with the time that was left.
  • Dismissing a toast is silent; it just goes.

Keys and focus

  • Showing a toast never moves focus.
  • F8 moves focus to the newest toast, and F8 again returns it. The section has aria-keyshortcuts="F8", and the read-out of a toast with an action ends with the way to it ("Press F8 for Undo"). Radix uses F8; on many Mac keyboards it needs Fn. A shortcut the project already has for this wins.
  • In a toast, Tab moves between its buttons and Escape dismisses it. Escape anywhere else is left to dialogs and menus.
  • When a toast with focus goes, focus moves to the newest other toast, or back to where it was before it entered the stack, by F8, Tab, or a click; F8 back does the same. When that element is gone or can't take focus (removed, disabled, hidden, or made inert), focus goes to the main content: <main> with tabindex="-1", the skip link's target. The script checks that focus really moved.
  • Each toast has a Dismiss button (an icon button named "Dismiss"), and its action is a button named by its visible text ("Undo").

The timers and the keys, which go with the stack's script:

// The timers pause while the stack is hovered or has focus, or the page is hidden, and go on with // the time that was left. F8 moves focus to the newest toast and back, and Escape dismisses the // toast that has focus. Goes with the stack's script. let hovered = false; const paused = () => hovered || region.contains(document.activeElement) || document.hidden;  // Starts or pauses every timer at once, keeping the time each toast has left function update() {   for (const [item, timer] of timers) {     if (paused() && timer.id) {       clearTimeout(timer.id);       timer.id = null;       timer.remaining -= Date.now() - timer.started;     } else if (!paused() && !timer.id) {       timer.started = Date.now();       timer.id = setTimeout(() => dismiss(item), timer.remaining);     }   } }  region.addEventListener('pointerenter', () => { hovered = true; update(); }); region.addEventListener('pointerleave', () => { hovered = false; update(); }); // However focus enters the stack (F8, Tab, a click), remember where it came from region.addEventListener('focusin', (event) => {   if (!region.contains(event.relatedTarget)) returnTo = event.relatedTarget;   update(); }); region.addEventListener('focusout', (event) => { if (!region.contains(event.relatedTarget)) update(); }); document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', update); document.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {   if (event.key === 'F8' && region.contains(document.activeElement)) {     restoreFocus();   } else if (event.key === 'F8' && list.lastElementChild) {     list.lastElementChild.focus();   } else if (event.key === 'Escape' && region.contains(event.target)) {     dismiss(event.target.closest('.toast'));   } else {     return;   }   event.preventDefault(); }); // A fixed bottom bar, in the page from the start (several things fixed at the bottom go in one) const bottomBar = document.querySelector('.bottom-bar');  // Scroll padding acts only when something scrolls, so when the stack or the bar appears or // changes, or the viewport shrinks, over the focused element, that element scrolls clear of both function keepFocusClear() {   const focused = document.activeElement;   if (region.hidden || !focused || focused === document.body || region.contains(focused) || bottomBar?.contains(focused)) return;   const a = focused.getBoundingClientRect();   const covers = (b) => a.bottom > b.top && a.top < b.bottom && a.right > b.left && a.left < b.right;   if ([region, bottomBar].some((element) => element && covers(element.getBoundingClientRect()))) focused.scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' }); } // The stack's height, with its 16 px gap and 8 px for a focus ring, for the padding new ResizeObserver(() => {   document.documentElement.style.setProperty('--toast-stack-height', `${region.hidden ? 0 : region.offsetHeight + 24}px`);   keepFocusClear(); }).observe(region); addEventListener('resize', keepFocusClear); visualViewport?.addEventListener('resize', keepFocusClear); // The bar's height (its border box, so padding counts) keeps the stack above it, and when the bar // appears, hides, or changes, focus scrolls clear if (bottomBar) new ResizeObserver(() => {   document.documentElement.style.setProperty('--bottom-bar-height', `${bottomBar.offsetHeight}px`);   keepFocusClear(); }).observe(bottomBar, { box: 'border-box' });

Phones and focus

  • On phones, toasts sit at the bottom, one at a time, and their buttons are at least 44 px.
  • Whatever scrolls the page gets a padding-bottom and a scroll-padding-bottom of a fixed bottom bar's height plus, while toasts show, the stack's height and room for a focus ring. That's :root usually; in an app whose page scrolls inside a container, it's that container, with box-sizing: border-box, since otherwise the padding makes a height: 100% container taller than the screen and nothing scrolls (checked). An element that gets focus then scrolls clear of the bar and the stack, and even a short page has room at the end to scroll its last element clear (checked). Where the project already keeps room for its bar at the end of the content, count it once.
  • Scroll padding acts only when something scrolls, so when a toast appears, the stack grows, the bar changes, or the viewport shrinks (the window, or an on-screen keyboard), and the stack or the bar comes over the element that already has focus, the script scrolls that element clear of both (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, in the page and in an app's scroll container). Focus inside the stack or the bar stays put.
  • The script measures the bar (.bottom-bar, the project's own selector) with a ResizeObserver on its border box, so padding counts: when the bar appears, hides (with hidden), or changes height, as when its text wraps or its padding makes room for a phone's home indicator, the stack moves above it, and the focused element scrolls clear of the stack and the bar, even when the bar grows past where the stack was (checked). The bar is in the page from the start, and several things fixed at the bottom, such as a tab bar and a cookie banner, go in one fixed container, which is what the script measures.
  • This covers the page scrolling, an app's scroll container, a fixed bottom bar, and changes of the viewport's size.
  • Swiping a toast away is optional; its Dismiss button does the same with a tap (2.5.7).

Motion

  • Motion is optional: a toast slides in over 250 ms and fades out over 200 ms. When one leaves, its wrapper's height collapses at the same time, so the others move into place without a jump. The snippet shows only the entrance.
  • Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, toasts appear and leave without moving; a short fade is fine.
  • A countdown bar is optional. It animates transform: scaleX(), not width, and pauses with the timer.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • Toasts 380 px wide (the screen less 32 px on phones), 12 to 16 px of padding, a 10 px radius, and 12 px apart.
  • Each variant has words and an icon, not only a color. Text meets 4.5:1 and icons 3:1 against the toast: on light tints, use the darkest shades for text (#14532d on #f0fdf4 is 8.7:1) and a dark shade for icons (#15803d, 4.8:1), since green-600 text on a green tint is only 3.0 to 3.2:1. Check the project's own colors in both themes.

Edge cases

  • Long text wraps; it's never cut off with an ellipsis.
  • Many toasts at once: three show, the rest wait in order, and the same message within a second or so shows once.
  • An action that fails, such as an Undo after the item is gone for good, shows its own error toast.
  • Toasts can be cleared when the page changes; errors stay.
  • Offline: one toast that stays while the connection is down, then a brief "Back online".

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Toasts are for brief news about something that just happened; errors people must fix show next to what they concern, and anything they must read before going on is a dialog
  • [ ] Two live regions, neither atomic, are in the page, empty, from the start and are never hidden: errors go to the alert region, everything else to the polite one
  • [ ] Each toast is read out once, its title and description together; a toast that waits for room is read out when it shows
  • [ ] Errors and toasts with an action stay until they're dismissed; the others leave after about 5 seconds
  • [ ] Timers pause while the stack is hovered or has focus, or the page is hidden, and go on with the time that was left
  • [ ] Showing a toast never moves focus
  • [ ] F8 moves focus to the newest toast and back, and the read-out of a toast with an action says so
  • [ ] Escape dismisses the toast that has focus and does nothing elsewhere
  • [ ] When a toast with focus goes, focus moves to the newest other toast, or back to where it was before it entered the stack, or to the main content when that element is gone or can't take focus
  • [ ] Every toast has a Dismiss button, and an action button named by its visible text
  • [ ] Toasts stack at the bottom, at most three at once (one on phones); the rest wait and show in order when there's room, and the toasts already showing stay when the screen narrows
  • [ ] While toasts show, neither the stack nor a fixed bottom bar hides the focused element, in the page or an app's scroll container: it scrolls clear of both when it gets focus, when a toast appears, when the viewport shrinks, and when the bar appears or changes height, with room at the end of the content for both; the stack sits above the bar and never covers the header
  • [ ] While a modal is open, the result of its task shows in the modal, since the page outside is inert
  • [ ] Long text wraps and is never cut off; text meets 4.5:1 and icons 3:1, and each variant has words and an icon, not only a color
  • [ ] Under reduced motion, toasts appear and leave without moving
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Modal Dialog: toasts sit below an open modal, and its task's results show in it.
  • Button: the action and Dismiss buttons.
  • Form Validation Pattern - UX and Timing Strategies: errors people must fix show by their fields, not in toasts.

These are suggestions; toasts work on their own.
excerpt: Toasts that screen readers announce and keyboard users can reach: live regions in the page from the start, Undo that stays until dismissed, timers that pause, F8 to the newest toast, and a stack that never covers what has focus.

title: Text Input Field
body:
Most forms succeed or fail in their text fields: people need to know what to enter, whether they have to, and what went wrong. This guide covers single-line inputs and multi-line text areas, built on the native <input> and <textarea>, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a text field component, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API.
  2. Otherwise use the native <input> with the type that matches the data, or <textarea> for more than one line, with a <label>.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Structure

  • Label: visible text in a <label for> that names the field. A placeholder is never the label.
  • Hint (optional): short help, such as the format or why the field is asked for.
  • Input: <input> or <textarea>.
  • Error: an element that's empty and hidden until there's an error.
  • Count (optional): for fields with a length limit.
  • Leading icon (optional): decoration, with aria-hidden="true".
  • Trailing button (optional): such as Clear or Show password, a real <button type="button"> with a name, at least 24 by 24 px (44 px suggested on touch).

Labels, hints, and required fields

  • The label is visible, and its text is the field's accessible name. A native <label for> is enough; use aria-labelledby only when the name has to come from elsewhere.
  • Say "required" or "optional" in words. When most fields are required, mark the optional ones "(optional)", and say so once at the top of the form: "All fields are required unless marked (optional)". If the design uses an asterisk, explain it at the top of the form, and don't color it like an error.
  • Put the native required attribute on required fields: screen readers announce it, and the form's validation reads it. When the app shows its own error messages, the form gets novalidate (see the Form Validation Pattern).
  • Hints are text below the label or the field, connected with aria-describedby. A placeholder disappears as soon as someone types, so it never holds the format or instructions. A placeholder that shows anything needed meets 4.5:1.

Errors

  • An error says what's wrong and how to fix it, such as "Enter an email address in the correct format, like name@example.com", in text next to the field, with an icon if the design uses one.
  • The error element stays in the field's aria-describedby, after the hint. With no error it's empty and hidden, so it adds nothing. While there's an error, the field has aria-invalid="true".
  • Field errors are never live regions (role="alert" or aria-live): on a submit, every field would announce at once. When errors are announced and where focus goes is the form's job (see the Form Validation Pattern).
  • Keep what the person typed; never clear a field because it's wrong.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<p>All fields are required unless marked (optional).</p> <div class="field">   <label for="email">Email address</label>   <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required     aria-describedby="email-hint email-error">   <p class="field-hint" id="email-hint">We'll send your receipt here.</p>   <p class="field-error" id="email-error" hidden></p> </div> <div class="field">   <label for="phone">Phone number (optional)</label>   <input id="phone" name="phone" type="tel" autocomplete="tel"     aria-describedby="phone-hint phone-error">   <p class="field-hint" id="phone-hint">Include the country code, for example +44 20 7946 0958.</p>   <p class="field-error" id="phone-error" hidden></p> </div> 
// Shows or clears a field's error. The error stays in aria-describedby, so it's read with the // field; cleared, it's empty and hidden and adds nothing. aria-invalid tells screen readers // that the value needs fixing. function setFieldError(input, message) {   const error = document.getElementById(`${input.id}-error`);   error.textContent = message;   error.hidden = !message;   if (message) input.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');   else input.removeAttribute('aria-invalid'); }

Types, autocomplete, and paste

  • Use the type that matches the data: email, tel, url, search, or password. It brings the right phone keyboard, and email and url a format check.
  • Codes, card numbers, and IDs are type="text" with inputmode="numeric", and one-time codes add autocomplete="one-time-code". type="number" is for quantities.
  • Fields that ask for the person's own data get the matching autocomplete token (WCAG 1.3.5), such as name, email, tel, street-address, postal-code, or bday. Passwords get current-password at sign-in and new-password when one is created.
  • Never block paste or autofill. Password managers and copied codes depend on them (WCAG 2.2 3.3.8).
  • Text is at least 16 px on phones: iOS Safari zooms the page when a smaller field gets focus.

Variants

  • Search: type="search", named "Search" by a visible or visually hidden label. Chromium and Firefox clear a search field on Escape themselves; no other field clears on Escape, since that would lose typing, and inside a dialog Escape closes the dialog. Chromium and WebKit also draw their own clear button in search fields, so a custom Clear button means hiding theirs (::-webkit-search-cancel-button).
  • Password: type="password" with the right autocomplete, spellcheck="false", and paste allowed. A Show password button is a toggle: its name stays "Show password", aria-pressed gives its state, and focus stays on it. The password is hidden again when the form is sent. The Login & Registration Forms guide has the full pattern.
  • Multi-line: <textarea> with the same label, hint, and error. It can grow with its content (field-sizing: content where supported).
  • Read-only: readonly keeps the value focusable, selectable, and sent with the form. disabled removes it from the Tab order and the form data, so use it only for fields that really can't be used yet, and say why in text.
  • Success (optional): only for checks the person can't see, such as an available username, with text such as "Username available". Not a green border and check on every valid field.

Length limits

  • Don't use maxlength for a limit people can reach. It cuts longer typed or pasted text without a word (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit), and stops typing without saying why.
  • Show the limit up front ("You can enter up to 200 characters"), count as people type ("You have 12 characters left"), and let them go over ("You have 30 characters too many"). Over the limit, the field is invalid until it's shortened, and the server checks the limit again.
  • The visible count changes on every keystroke; screen readers hear it once typing pauses, through one status region.
  • Count characters the way the server does. The snippet counts code points, so an emoji counts as one.
